A geometric geometric T-duality is demonstrated for a class of tori equipped with twisted fibres, resulting in a straightforward transformation of their worldvolume supersymmetric effective actions. It is found that geometric T-duality preserves the string theory disk partition function and the supersymmetric effective action of the associated Wess-Zumino terms, and reduces the calculation of twisted geometric BPS states to classical methods. Furthermore, this geometric T-duality is applied to a range of examples, including tori with orbifold points and combined geometric T- and S-dualities, yielding novel solutions to the associated Mathieu equation. These geometric T-duality transformations are also found to encompass the established electric/magnetic duality principle. The study also explores potential applications of geometric T-duality in addressing open problems related to geometric quantization and the calculations of BPS states. Lastly, it is suggested that geometric T-duality could serve as a bridge connecting M-theory to string theory. The research concludes by proposing several general conjectures based on the findings. Additionally, some supplementary observations and possibilities are mentioned.

This research focuses on enhancing autonomous vehicles' ability to collaborate by sharing information during drives. To achieve this, we developed a novel approach where vehicles learn to recognize when fellow drivers are observing specific situations and adapt their behavior accordingly. Importantly, our method doesn't rely on expert input; instead, vehicles within a group learn from each other through mutual observations. We thoroughly tested our approach on various traffic scenarios and found that it allows vehicles to quickly learn and respond within 10-20 seconds, even in situations where they frequently encounter each other, such as at intersections. Results indicate that vehicles using our method are better equipped to navigate and interact with others effectively. Additionally, we found that our approach is resistant to interference from other vehicles and can easily adapt to new and unusual situations. Finally, experiments using a simulation tool showed that vehicles using our method can reduce their speed and avoid collisions when encountering potential hazards shared by other drivers. This includes scenarios involving pedestrians, cyclists, and other vehicles. To validate our approach, we also conducted physical vehicle tests and found that it performs as expected in real-world driving conditions. Specifically, vehicles using our method can respond within 1 second in physical tests, which is comparable to our simulated results. Overall, our approach allows vehicles to quickly learn, collaborate effectively, and respond to various situations through mutual observations. This includes recognizing when fellow drivers are observing specific situations and adapting their behavior accordingly. This collaborative behavior is crucial for safe and efficient traffic flow and can be applied to various robotic platforms beyond autonomous vehicles. With further refinement, this research has the potential to improve the ecological efficiency of robotic systems by encouraging cooperation among group members. In everyday life, people often observe and learn from others' physical interactions with objects, which we then apply to our own interactions. Similarly, a computer vision system should be able to learn and track the physical relationships between objects as they appear in a time-series of 3D point clouds, which we then use to predict future interactions. To build a robust model for predicting interactions, we've created a new dataset containing 3D point clouds from real-world video footage, which capture the intricate details of human physical interactions with everyday objects. This dataset, called HOKE, contains 1,000 sequences of 20 different objects, which were scanned using depth sensors to provide accurate spatial data for analysis. Our model has been tested and shown to perform better than other competing models, which we then compared to human predictions in an attention experiment. This research investigates non-Gaussian characteristics of laser-cooled particles in an innovative, dissipative optical grid cooling technique. This research delves into the underlying connections among cryptocurrencies by examining both their pairwise and higher-order interdependencies with other markets. Our findings reveal that, on one hand, there is substantial evidence supporting the theory that most cryptocurrencies are influenced by specific underlying assets, primarily Bitcoin. On the other hand, when we investigate the collective behavior of higher-order relationships, we discover that the structure of the cryptocurrency network is dominated by a core group centered around Bitcoin. Interestingly, certain alternative cryptocurrencies appear to benefit from this core position, with our results indicating that their performance is more accurately predicted when considering their relationships with other markets in addition to Bitcoin. Ultimately, our results provide valuable insights for investors and portfolio managers, enabling them to better understand and analyze the complex dynamics of the cryptocurrency market. Furthermore, our research offers a fresh perspective on the cryptocurrency system as a whole, with potential implications for the development of future digital currencies. Lastly, our results serve as a useful resource for researchers, outlining a systematic approach to investigating the characteristics of digital systems; this approach may be adapted for studying other digital ecosystems. The impact of incorporating quantum mechanics at the molecular level within large systems, such as droplets and aerosols, is generally being overlooked. Using ab initio path integral molecular dynamics at the temperatures of supercooled cloud conditions, we investigate the role of zero-point motion in sulfuric acid dimer and tetramer complexes, comparing it to their corresponding classical behavior. While the quantum nature has a noticeable effect on the potential energy, it diminishes when considering kinetic energy and bond lengths. Notably, the presence of zero-point motion significantly influences the potential energy, leading to the formation of more stable acid-base pairs in smaller clusters, potentially contributing to new nucleation pathways. These findings underscore the necessity of accounting for quantum effects in modeling the nucleation processes of specific systems. -Author's Abstract

in capturing the full range of human perception.
Recent breakthroughs in GANs and data-driven methodologies have led to breakthroughs in music generation,
but reliable evaluation remains a challenge.
This study investigates the efficacy of data augmentation in improving the performance of neural networks
in evaluating music compositions through various techniques, revealing that applying GAN-generated data
to training can significantly boost results, with particular success when combining multiple methods. 
Notably, using a Transformer architecture yields the most substantial improvement when incorporating
augmented data, outperforming other networks even when trained on augmented data alone. 
Our findings provide new insights into music composition evaluation using neural networks and data augmentation. 
Additionally, the developed music augmentation tool can be utilized for future research, given its versatility
in generating diverse music samples that are difficult for humans to distinguish from genuine compositions. 
The proposed approach is also expected to contribute to the creation of more sophisticated music generation systems.

A prospective framework examines how opportunities unfold over time, in contrast to retrospective approaches. We develop a model to understand how prospects are distributed across different social groups within a dynamic time framework, influenced by past events. Our findings reveal how considerations of past events, when reflected in current prospects, can lead to perceived inequalities that persist over time, even though they may appear to disappear in a retrospective view. Furthermore, variations in the duration of prospects and memories can result in perceived inequalities that vary with time, as well as in perceived inequalities related to age or generational cohorts. Ultimately, only a specific duration, which we identify through a balance between risk and memory, can lead to perceived stability of mobility prospects over time. When this balance is not achieved, mobility prospects may appear to change over time, even though they remain unchanged. For instance, if individuals place greater importance on long-term risks, mobility prospects may appear to improve over time, whereas a focus on short-term memories may lead to perceived declines in mobility prospects over time. Our theoretical results are supported by empirical analysis of data from the United States, demonstrating that mobility prospects do indeed appear to change over time, as well as in perceived mobility prospects in South Africa, as reported in public surveys. Our research thus highlights the distinct insights that prospective and dynamic perspectives can offer in understanding social mobility. Moreover, it also underscores the importance of considering how opportunities unfold and are perceived over time when examining intergenerational mobility. At the very least, our findings suggest that mobility policies focused solely on retrospective perspectives may not be sufficient to address perceived inequalities in mobility prospects over extended periods of time. Rather, they may need to be complemented by policies that directly influence how opportunities are distributed across different social groups or how prospects are perceived over time. Our model can be adapted to examine how different policies, such as education or taxation, shape prospects and distribute prospects in various social groups, as well as how past events influence current prospects. Our research thus provides a framework to understand how various policies can address perceived inequalities in mobility prospects over long periods of time. We introduce a measure called space toughness to evaluate a solver's ability to tackle complex systems of linear equations. This metric surpasses traditional benchmarks in assessing a solver's performance on equation systems, as it directly correlates with the solver's memory consumption. We demonstrate the effectiveness of space toughness through case studies involving sparse systems, showcasing its ability to accurately predict and prioritize challenges posed by hyperbolic partial differential equations, ill-conditioned elliptic problems, and systems generated randomly. Furthermore, space toughness serves as a reliable indicator of a solver's instability in the context of backward time integration, especially when near singular or positive semi-definite systems. By utilizing space toughness, researchers can systematically identify and address performance and reliability issues in solvers, ultimately leading to substantial improvements. Previous initiatives led to the creation of the Hebrew Universal Dependencies treebank, 
though it suffered from data deficiencies, notably a severe lack of training data for Modern Hebrew.
This problem is addressed by our work, which employs a cutting-edge NLP framework to generate enhanced annotations 
for various text categories, ultimately resulting in improved UD annotations and increased availability of resources for NLP within Israel. 
The updated resource comprises 13,000 sentences, offering valuable opportunities for NLP researchers and practitioners. 
The associated data, software and documentation are freely accessible at https://github.com/he-ud/ud-hebrew-v2.4.0. 
This project builds on the foundations laid by earlier surges in Hebrew UD treebanking, specifically the work of Flatt et al. (2018) and
Katz et al. (2020), who contributed significantly to the field. 
Conversely, this project draws inspiration and support from the community that has been waiting for these developments, 
notably from NLP researchers and practitioners at the Israeli Data Science Conference. 
Our efforts aim to promote standardization in NLP annotations, facilitate data sharing and collaboration, 
and ultimately accelerate the advancement of NLP models with real-world applications. 
In particular, the enhanced Hebrew UD treebank is now equipped to support NLP models with improved performance in domains such as law and medicine. 
The success of this initiative could serve as a model for enhancing and expanding NLP resources in Israel and potentially elsewhere in the region. 
Our work has been successfully evaluated using standard metrics, including UAS, LAS and F1 scores, 
and the associated results indicate a substantial 5-6% increase in parsing accuracy across 8 diverse text categories. 
Our research also explores the benefits of fine-tuning models on data from relevant domains, 
notably law and medicine, which yield notable improvements of 3-4% in parsing accuracy when applied to data from the same domains. 
Conversely, models fine-tuned on general Modern Hebrew data may still perform satisfactorily on data from other domains, 
though with slightly lower accuracy compared to domain-specific fine-tuning. 
Our research contributes to the ongoing development of NLP models with real-world applications and 
advances the state-of-the-art in UD Hebrew parsing, as evidenced by our results and the enhanced resource, which is now freely accessible at https://github.com/he-ud/ud-hebrew-v2.4.0.

This safety net enables automatic emergency braking and has been successfully implemented on a Stratus vehicle platform. Developed by the Laboratory Alliance for Automotive Safety, this Prognostic Safety System was built using System Level Synthesis techniques and utilizes a combination of model predictive control and prognostics in an innovative safety algorithm. This safety net is triggered only when there's a perceived threat and can be adjusted to suit various automotive applications. This paper will present the design and testing of this safety net. To test its effectiveness, the safety net was integrated into a vehicle simulation environment and put through a series of driving scenarios that simulated real-world conditions, such as driving on roads with obstacles or encountering other vehicles. This allowed for a thorough evaluation of the safety net's performance and any potential limitations. The results showed that the safety net successfully prevented accidents in all tests and provided adequate warning times. This pioneering work marks a significant step towards ensuring vehicle safety and setting new standards for Advanced Driver Assistance Systems. Recent research has uncovered a phenomenon where large language models can learn in context, leading to comparable outcomes under specific conditions. In this study, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of how various training datasets impact this in-context learning phenomenon. Our analysis indicates that models trained on diverse datasets are more likely to exhibit in-context learning on unrelated tasks. Furthermore, we observed a significant correlation between the level of semantic change within a task's input context and in-context learning performance. Notably, our findings suggest that models developed with a broad training dataset can adapt to tasks requiring significant input modifications. Conversely, models trained solely on a single domain may not display in-context learning when faced with substantial input changes. To illustrate this point, we employed the movie title domain and discovered that models trained solely on movie titles are more likely to exhibit in-context learning when prompted with nearby titles but are more adaptable to tasks involving more drastic changes. Our research provides insights into the relationship between pretraining datasets and in-context learning. Our code and pre-trained models are available for public access at https://github.com/ghildiny/lm_in_context. This research was supported by the ANR (French National Research Agency) through the ANADIA project.

Additionally, the scattering amplitudes' low-energy expansion aligns with Einstein gravity's predictions, including the presence of polygravitons. The success of future Fifth-Generation (5G) wireless systems depends on their ability to minimize their environmental impact without compromising performance.  To achieve this, 5G architectures with self-organizing capabilities are being developed, allowing for dynamic changes in their structure and operation.  To effectively manage and maintain these dynamic systems, 5G administrators will need to implement special procedures.  This paper proposes a set of core administrative processes for 5G networks to facilitate changes during operation, including processes for handling errors, activating new functionality, and enhancing existing or deploying new services.  To validate these processes, we have developed two use cases based on realistic scenarios and have simulated them using a tool called Netfab.  The results show that, with the right processes in place, 5G administrators can take full advantage of their system's self-organizing features, leading to improved performance and reduced energy consumption.  Overall, this work contributes to the knowledge of 5G administrative processes and provides a useful resource for system designers and administrators.  Finally, the source code for the Netfab simulator is available for free on GitHub at the specified link.

To ensure the synthesized speech has a natural flow, the transition between adjacent units is optimized. The system's effectiveness is evaluated through both subjective and objective assessments of its output. Notably, when compared to systems that utilize transcripts obtained through automatic speech recognition, the naturalness and intelligibility of our approach remain comparable across board platforms, and even surpasses it on certain platforms. A novel new approach to motion planning is presented, utilizing connected convex optimization and data-driven McCormick envelope relaxation for predicting plant behavior. This method, MLCP, leverages minimal system knowledge and relies on experimental data to forecast transient responses, using linked variables representing time stages and constraints derived from safety considerations to ensure real-world applicability. To enhance solution efficiency, MLCP incorporates an incremental solution strategy, providing a practical solution for complex planning issues. This approach was successfully validated on an actual drone and in a simulated 3D racing environment. MLCP offers a versatile solution for optimizing control systems, applicable to a wide range of domains including autonomous vehicles and robotic systems. This general framework enables motion planning with varied performance trade-offs and allows for easy adaptation to evolving system conditions or performance metric adjustments without re-formulating the optimization problem. The rotation of coffee beans within a brewing method known as the Aeropress is examined, along with the effects of gravitational force on its spinning motion. 
The torque applied by the liquid surface causes the beans to move in a chaotic, irregular pattern, which under certain conditions can be modeled as a driven pendulum motion. 
This pendulum motion is subject to driving force and gravitational force, influencing its trajectory.
The height of the pendulum is linked to the method's design and can be adjusted to alter the system's behavior. 
By accurately calculating the pendulum's constants, the dynamics of the swinging motion can be better understood, allowing for optimized brewing to be achieved. 
The research also explores how variations in coffee bean size affect the system's behavior and identifies a critical parameter for evaluating the swirling pattern in closed drive systems. 
Ultimately, the findings enable the modification of the Aeropress to reproduce a range of swirling patterns in coffee, from weak and uniform to strong and bead-like in shape. 
The methodology employed can be applied to analyzing the spinning motions in other driven systems and may have broader implications in understanding the behavior of top-heavy objects. 
The results are documented in a study published in the journal Physical Review X under the title "Swirling in Coffee as a Driven Pendulum," featuring contributions from J. A. C. G. and M. A. C. G. as co-authors.

The numerical simulations were conducted using Mathematica, a computational software.

We introduce a new decentralized learning method that leverages a notion of similarity between data distributions to enhance robustness in the presence of heterogeneous data. Building on the standard decentralized stochastic gradient descent algorithm, we enhance it with a corrective term that adjusts the learning rate based on the relative distributions of neighboring nodes. By maintaining an estimate of local distribution shifts, we are able to provide global convergence guarantees for our method. Experimental results demonstrate that the new algorithm achieves improved robustness and accelerated convergence compared to traditional methods, particularly in scenarios with significant distributional variations among nodes. The implementation details and synthetic data demo are freely available on GitHub. Furthermore, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the results, which can be found in the supplementary material. This research is currently unpublished.

The interplay of light and matter, captured through the dipole radiator, offers a simplified approach to understanding phenomena like absorption, emission, and scattering in optical physics applied to solid-state physics. However, this approximation is not always feasible due to complex system requirements, such as near-field effects or customized photon properties. The ability to replace the exact dipole-radiator description with this model, while maintaining physical consistency, is therefore valuable. Notably, this approximation remains reliable for isolated systems but lacks proven invariance under transformations that preserve their physical properties, such as rotation and translation. The validation of this approximation for a specific type of tight-binding model, derived from first-principle quantum models, addresses this shortcoming and paves the way for the use of simpler dipole models in complex solid-state systems. The code used to develop this validation, specifically using the PyTight library, is also available on GitHub for public access. Furthermore, our findings provide a basis for the inductive validation of such approximations, enabling the automation of such validation processes in the future. Lastly, the study suggests a potential application of our approach in the context of nanophotonics. This research introduces an advanced computer vision technique that can accurately identify and locate three-dimensional objects within a two-dimensional image, even when some key points are missing, as happens in real-world challenges like predicting object shapes from a single image. Additionally, our study presents a new 3D object reconstruction task that focuses on predicting an object's overall shape based on its semantic characteristics, rather than its complete geometric structure. To tackle these complex problems, we have developed two new datasets containing detailed information about vehicle types and their physical structures. Our dataset includes comprehensive annotations for over 400,000 images and 1.5 million keypoints, which provide a rich understanding of object forms. Our technique, dubbed Category-level Object-Pose-and-Form Estimation (COPFE), employs a neural network that can handle partial keypoint information and relies on an iterative process to generate accurate three-dimensional reconstructions from two-dimensional images. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of COPFE in predicting object shapes from single images and utilizing partial keypoint information to analyze 3D objects. Our approach prioritizes resilience and can function effectively even when some key points are missing. Furthermore, COPFE is designed to learn an object's overall shape, which is essential for creating intuitive and versatile robotic systems that interact with the world. Our research also addresses the resilient object-pose estimation problem and showcases the utility of our technique in real-world challenges, as validated by extensive experiments. Our datasets and implementation are open-source and available for public use at the specified links. Our research aims to advance the field of computer vision by promoting the development of more accessible and adaptable vision systems. When dealing with the Cauchy distribution, constructing intervals for estimating individual parameters $\gamma$ and $\delta$ in the model $X_t = \gamma + \delta t + \sqrt{1+\gamma^2}W_t$ proves to be a difficult task, due to the lack of sufficient regularity. However, by employing a semi-parametric approach based on the non-parametric estimation of $\gamma$ and $\delta$, we are able to establish the asymptotic normal distribution needed for creating confidence intervals and regions, thereby addressing this challenge. The proposed method is then validated through simulations and comparative tests, showing its effectiveness in the context of the Cauchy model. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical justification for its reliability by establishing the consistency of our estimator and proving its asymptotic normal distribution in a more general model that encompasses the Cauchy case, including cases with zero noise. The method is further demonstrated on a historical dataset of wind speed observations and compared with other non-parametric approaches. A new clinical trial design known as the basket trial has gained popularity in recent years. This design involves conducting a single trial across multiple diseases driven by a shared biological hypothesis. The primary goal of basket trials not only yields insights into the target indication with the highest statistical power but also provides opportunities to explore secondary benefits and combine data from various patient subgroups. The conventional sample size calculation methods in basket trials treat each patient subgroup as independent events. However, our study aims to investigate whether it is possible to utilize data from other subgroups to enhance statistical power in detecting treatment effects. We have developed a Bayesian approach for estimating required trial sizes that allows subgroups to borrow statistical strength from one another by sharing data. The results from our simulations indicate that our proposed method can significantly reduce the required trial size by up to 70% and is particularly beneficial in trials involving multiple subgroups. The method also retains 100% of the power to detect a treatment effect exclusive to a single subgroup. We have successfully applied our method in a real-world scenario involving a basket trial aimed at evaluating the efficacy and safety of a cancer immunotherapy known as pembrolizumab in various patient subgroups. The details of our method, along with the real-world application, are presented in a step-by-step format to facilitate its implementation in clinical trial design. The method can be accessed through the R package named BayesBayes. Further research is needed to refine our method and assess its practical usability in clinical trial design. In particular, we plan to investigate the impact of varying data quality across different patient subgroups and the potential risks of overestimating treatment effects due to shared data between subgroups. The findings from our study will be presented at the 2022 ISBS Conference in Tokyo, Japan. The goal of this research is to increase the efficiency and reliability of high-speed motion systems by using advanced linear parameter-varying (LPV) technology to enhance closed-loop performance and extend operational ranges. Traditional sequential loop closure methods are limited in their ability to achieve high precision due to variations in system parameters, but this study develops an LPV sequential closure algorithm that prioritizes high precision throughout the operational range. The algorithm utilizes online parameter estimation to minimize uncertainties and ensures the system remains within safe parameter boundaries. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulation results, which show significant improvements in high-speed motion systems, even in cases where large operational ranges are involved. Furthermore, the LPV sequential closure algorithm can serve as a motion controller and safety controller in one integrated unit, simplifying system integration and operation. The key benefit of this controller is its ability to seamlessly transition between motion tasks and ensure safe system operation, characteristics that are critical in the practical application of this research. The simulated performance outcomes of this LPV sequential closure algorithm align with actual test data from a high-accuracy motion system, which validates the algorithm's potential for real-world application. The core outcomes of this research are documented in two patent applications, highlighting their potential for commercial use in high-accuracy motion systems. The primary software tool utilized in this research was Simulink, which enabled the development of an integrated system model incorporating LPV technology, sequential loop closure, and real-time online parameter estimation. The resulting model was then utilized to implement the LPV sequential closure algorithm through automatic code generation. The key hardware component evaluated in this research was a high-accuracy motion system, which was tested using a standardized step test to validate the LPV sequential closure algorithm's performance. The key outcome of this research is the LPV sequential closure algorithm itself, which has the potential to enhance the efficiency and reliability of high-speed motion systems. The core outcome of this research was also presented at the 2021 American Control Conference. We introduce a novel deep learning network called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed to perform partial-to-partial object alignment from unregistered 3D models even in the absence of visible surfaces. These alignments can have numerous applications in computer vision and graphics, such as tracking deforming, occluded objects like human bodies even in a single viewpoint. The key challenge lies in directly utilizing point cloud information to create robust and efficient learning strategies. Our approach builds upon a self-supervised keypoint-based learning method which not only preserves corresponding keypoints during alignment but also maintains the overall shape structure in a geometrically intuitive manner. Through extensive testing on the widely-used Human3.6M dataset, we demonstrate that our PRNet delivers more accurate pose predictions compared to traditional and cutting-edge deformation and alignment models, even at a remarkably high speed of 10 frames per second per image pair. Our code and dataset reproduction resources will be made available. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset called DeformPIE, containing over 36,000 human body pose images captured from multiple viewpoints, which can serve as a valuable resource for developing novel deformation and alignment models. Our PRNet has been successfully applied to generate realistic and deformable human avatars for animation purposes. Ultimately, DeformPIE and PRNet represent a powerful collaborative framework, providing numerous potential applications in various areas of computer research and technology. This approach leverages a gradient-free optimization technique to counteract limitations inherent in traditional trajectory-based simulation methods, such as a susceptibility to diverging trajectories that worsen with time, and a requirement for excessive computational resources. In this paper, we use the Fourier transform to demonstrate the non-trivial, non-continuous nature of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, including its non-continuous non-triviality within the distribution space. This analysis also provides new insights into the continuity of Toeplitz operators with symbols from modulation spaces. Furthermore, we extend the Gelfand-Shilov space to a larger space, defined by multiple decay and smoothness conditions, while preserving its key properties. This includes being a Frechet space with continuous inclusions and a generalization of the Schwartz space. This larger space can be seen as a compromise between the Gelfand-Shilov space and the Sjoestrand class. Moreover, we extend modulation spaces to their modulation-Sjostrand space counterparts, and examine their relationships with extended Gelfand-Shilov spaces and the boundedness of Toeplitz operators with these symbols. Deep learning techniques have achieved significant success in domain adaptation (DA) tasks, but they pose challenges when dealing with large source domains or when their data is not readily available. This research aims to address these issues by employing unsupervised instance adaptation (UIA) which enables data transformation from one domain to another without knowledge of class labels. Furthermore, UIA can facilitate downstream tasks by generating synthetic data for enhanced representation learning. To improve UIA's effectiveness, our method partitions source domain data into individual instances before training domain-specific models, allowing each to learn from isolated samples instead of mixed domain data. We also introduce a cyclic division generative adversarial network (CDGAN) to generate synthetic data for source domain samples, producing pseudo-labels that guide downstream classification. Our experiments on two datasets demonstrate that our UIA approach outperforms conventional domain adaptation methods, while CDGAN enhances representation learning through synthetic data augmentation. Deep learning-based speech enhancement models are typically evaluated using a specific setup, where the input audio signal is artificially distorted and then reconstructed through a designated process, with the desired speech signal as the target output. Nevertheless, this setup's strict assumptions aren't always met in real-world scenarios, particularly with regards to the presence of background noise. In our analysis, we examine the impact of ground noise on speech enhancement models, where ground noise refers to steady background noise present throughout the signal. Our findings indicate that current deep learning-based approaches struggle to effectively handle such noise, leading to deteriorated reconstruction quality in its presence. In contrast, a modified evaluation protocol that accounts for variable noise levels yields more favorable results, suggesting that deep learning-based methods can mitigate ground noise to a limited extent. Our study also highlights the importance of considering multiple scenarios in evaluating speech enhancement models, as these models are ultimately designed to improve speech quality in diverse, real-world environments. Our dataset is comprised of multiple noise types and can be accessed at https://se-nd.speech.shef.ac.uk/. Our research is centered around enhancing speech quality in noisy environments and could have practical applications in areas like mobile phone design, where users frequently interact with speech through these devices. Ultimately, we hope to develop a speech enhancement model capable of effectively mitigating ground noise and improving overall speech quality in diverse, real-world scenarios. Our work is particularly relevant to the fields of speech enhancement and source separation, as speech quality in noisy environments is ultimately a reflection of the underlying audio signal's quality. Let G be a noncompact arithmetic subgroup of isometries in a Busemann-Poincaré space. We establish two key results: First, G's geometrically finite actions are characterized by G's commutative subgroup membership, thereby proving G's charmability. Second, combining G's arithmetic and irreducible representations, we derive G's rigidity by showing the equivalence between G's irreducibility and G's complicity in a commutative group. These findings significantly broaden earlier works by Sun, Chen-M\"uller-Schmidt and Horbez-M\"uller-Schmidt. Additionally, for noncompact arithmetic subgroups of isometries in a Busemann-Poincar\'e space, our theorems yield new proofs of Serre's rigidity theorem and Maschler's charmability theorem, respectively. Furthermore, applying G's rigidity to noncompact arithmetic groups in Busemann-Poincar\'e spaces, we establish a Maschler-type corollary. Lastly, our work includes a few complementary observations and questions. Ultimately, this document aims to provide a comprehensive overview of arithmetic group theory's current state and potential future developments. Due to article length constraints, proofs are presented in the arXiv document 2201.04615. Instead, we focus here on introducing key concepts and outlining our main results and their implications. This study presents an extension of a driving system designed to fail safely, 
building upon the work of [Babaioff et al., 2019], with each component failing 
in a way that doesn't cause harm to the driver and passengers. To guarantee this 
fail-safe behavior, we employed formal methods to thoroughly verify the system's 
performance in the event of a failure. This involved developing models for 
electrical and thermal dysfunction, as well as comparing the results with an 
existing safety standard (ISO 26262). Due to the vast number of potential failure 
scenarios, we developed an automated tool to quickly identify and prioritize these 
failures based on their likelihood and potential impact on the vehicle's operation. 
Ultimately, our analysis showed that the modified system could safely fail in all 
possible failure scenarios, with its performance meeting the requirements of ISO 
26262. This research offers a valuable resource for designers and developers, 
outlining a systematic approach to identifying and mitigating failures in the design 
phase, thereby reducing the likelihood and impact of malfunctions on vehicle safety 
and reliability. Additionally, our work provides an example of how to apply formal 
methods in the automotive industry to ensure the safe failure of electronic control 
units, as required by ISO 26262. This study was partially funded by a grant from 
Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (NSERC) and supported by 
Infineon Technologies Agileinus GmbH. It has been accepted for publication at the 
32nd International Conference on Tools and Algorithms for the Construction and 
Analysis of Systems (TACAS). A preprint is available at arXiv:2306.09023. For 
more information on this research, please visit https://formal-automotive.github.io. 
This website provides access to the source code, models, and tools used in this 
study, with the aim of promoting transparency and reproducibility in formal 
verification. Furthermore, a video summarizing this research is available at

delighted to receive any feedback or suggestions on improving this research. They

Numerous applications in science and engineering involve tracking objects or entities across various stages or conditions, which can be modeled using cluster analysis for clearer visualization and understanding. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to clustering based on impacts, which offers more accurate results by leveraging trajectory data and dynamic system models, ultimately providing insights beyond what data alone can offer. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through clustering simulations of lunar, asteroid, and comet orbits, as well as dynamical systems with either one or two dimensions. Additionally, we showcase its application in identifying cometary families using actual comet trajectory data. Furthermore, we highlight the inherent benefits and trade-offs of this clustering method compared to existing techniques. Lastly, we propose potential future research directions based on the findings of this study. Key source codes are available on GitHub for reproduction of the results. This essay explores three mathematical approaches to understanding Leibnizian calculus, all of which focus on the conceptual foundations of infinitesimal analysis as developed by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.  The first approach, based on the work of Richard Josephz Mantassel, views Leibnizian calculus as a product of the "augment" method, a technique which was central to the development of geometrical reasoning during the 17th and early 18th centuries.  This approach is contrasted with two alternative perspectives, one proposed by Jon R. Michaels and the other by Stuart Anderson, both of which emphasize the role of the "method of generation" in shaping Leibnizian thought.  A key challenge arising from these different interpretations revolves around the issue of how they might be resolved into a unified understanding of Leibnizian calculus.  Furthermore, questions surrounding the relevance of these foundational ideas to the broader philosophical framework of Leibnizian monadology also demand attention.  Ultimately, this essay seeks to demonstrate that each of these three interpretations possesses intrinsic value, and can thus contribute to a richer understanding of the historical context in which the fundamental concepts of calculus were forged.  In addition, this essay also seeks to illustrate that each of these three interpretations possesses a contemporary analogue within the broader context of modern mathematics, and that these analogues serve to underscore their individual strengths and merits.  By highlighting these parallels, this essay aims to show that the foundational ideas of calculus, as they were developed by Leibniz and his contemporaries, retain a continued relevance to the broader philosophical framework of calculus in the 21st century. Conducting large-scale HI intensity mapping experiments involves measuring the diffuse gas within the early universe, but achieving this requires overcoming radio interference from human activities.  Despite the widespread issue, there's a lack of comprehensive research on its impact, so we developed a theoretical framework using a linearized map comparison technique.  Our method involves analyzing how radio interference affects HI intensity maps by utilizing a spatial perturbation series up to the third order.  We applied our approach to the data from the First Large Array for the Detection of Hydrogen at Low frequencies (FLAGSHIP) pilot experiment, which operates at 190 MHz, covering approximately 13,000 square degrees on the sky.  After removing radio interference using our technique, we removed the resulting systematic effects from the maps, revealing a slight underestimation of the HI power spectrum at the 1σ level for small angular scales and a slight overestimation at larger scales.  However, this underestimation is largely mitigated when using higher-order maps to analyze the HI power spectrum.  We also found that removing radio interference has a minimal impact on the HI power spectrum, but further testing is required to confirm our findings.  We plan to implement this technique in the upcoming MWA HI21CM Project, which will operate at 154 MHz and cover 18,000 square degrees on the sky.  We anticipate that removing radio interference using our technique will improve the HI power spectrum recovery by up to 10%. The integration of implicit feedback and explicit feedback is crucial in addressing personalization's core challenge, which is accurately predicting users' preferences. While implicit feedback-based models using collaborative filtering excel at predicting user behavior patterns, they struggle to capture rich content details. Conversely, models using collaborative filtering in conjunction with content-based techniques can tap into both user behavior patterns and content characteristics, thus offering enhanced predictive capabilities. However, such an approach is only feasible when content data is readily available. We therefore developed a two-part recommender system, comprising of an implicit feedback-based model and a content-based model built on the BERT framework, to handle scenarios with and without rich content information respectively. Our research focuses on the domain of digital learning platforms, where users engage with course materials and instructors. We employed a two-stage ranking process that combines the predictions from both models, weighing them equally. We evaluated our system against various baseline models and observed a 3.1% increase in click-through rate and a 1.6% enhancement in predicted user ratings compared to the model without content-based component. Furthermore, our analysis on user groups revealed that the content-based component yields the most significant improvement in predictive capabilities among users with higher levels of engagement in the platform. We have made our source code publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/DeepLearningUI/CCF2022-DLBP-Challenge-4. We believe our approach can serve as a valuable resource for enhancing digital learning platforms' recommender systems, thus leading to improved user experience and increased system engagement. We also successfully participated in the 2022 DLBP competition, where our paper was awarded the 2nd place. The GRAVITY capture camera is a high-tech device employing an adaptive optics system and image reconstruction techniques to capture and reassemble data from four to eight telemetry channels of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, thereby optimizing its sensitivity and spatial resolution. With the aid of this system, which was introduced in 2017, GRAVITY has achieved its full design potential on a range of objects, including those with intrinsic fine details and those exhibiting variability. This paper outlines the design and operational efficiency of the capture camera and presents recent observational outcomes, showcasing its capabilities to span an extended range of spatial resolutions and fringe visibility. Additionally, we detail our approach to optimizing the capture camera for high signal-to-noise ratio observations and describe novel enhancements that will facilitate the forthcoming second generation of the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope Array, including a new flexible interface capable of seamlessly interfacing with the software framework Nautilus and the data reduction pipeline ESODI for analysis. We also outline our plans to integrate these enhancements into the capture camera system. Finally, we present preliminary results from observations of several objects under diverse conditions using the enhanced capture camera setup. These results indicate a significant improvement in its performance, thereby paving the way for the future success of the second generation of the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope Array. Researchers have developed efficient algorithms for this problem, but these solutions don't work on graphs with a highway measure. Although some modified versions of the problem with additional constraints have been studied, the basic $k$-center problem with exit nodes has yet to be fully addressed. We now provide an efficient algorithm for this more complex problem, which includes exit nodes, and our solution improves upon previous work by allowing larger exit radii with the same time complexity. This paper delves into the capacity of the graph convolutional network (GCN) in forecasting multi-dimensional time series data. Our investigation reveals through experimental analysis that employing a fully connected synthetic technical indicators (STI) can actually impede a GCN's ability to provide accurate forecasts for the underlying system it is derived from. This unintended consequence motivates the development of an adaptive GCN structure, incorporating resources-aware nodes, where connectivity is determined based on data properties and resources availability in resource-constrained edge computing environments. The proposed approach utilizes the STI indicators only where they enhance a GCN's predictive capabilities, while also being resource-efficient by virtue of reduced required resources for computation at the edge. Results obtained demonstrate the adaptive GCN's superiority over its baseline fully connected counterpart in forecasting solar irradiance when integrated with photovoltaic systems. Furthermore, this approach showcases its ability to provide reliable forecasts for complex systems despite resource constraints at the edge. Consequently, this approach has far-reaching implications for forecasting complex systems and can be applied across a wide range of domains. Ground-based telescopes are limited by the scattering of light through Earth's atmosphere, especially at blue wavelengths. To improve on-ground observations, accurate models of atmospheric scattering are necessary, but current models have not been directly validated against real data. We have developed a new method to determine the parameters of these models by comparing their predictions against observed spectra from various wavelengths and targets. Applying this method to observed spectra from different sites at different times, we found that while certain atmospheric models share similar properties, others have site-specific characteristics that require individual interpretation. We found no blue-scattering peak at our primary site, but rather a flat profile, suggesting that while the scattering peak is typically around 450 nm according to some models, this may not always be the case. We also found that while certain models share similar properties, others have unique characteristics and should not be used interchangeably. We found no direct correlation between temperature or humidity and atmospheric scattering, but rather site-specific and variable conditions. These results will help improve our understanding and modeling of atmospheric scattering to better represent its effects on ground-based observations. Recently, pre-trained models have achieved remarkable success in various educational datasets, however, the cost associated with relying on high-quality pre-trained models is the requirement of a large training dataset which includes labeled data from multiple instructors, a challenging and resource-intensive task to accomplish. To overcome this obstacle, we suggest a novel approach called PILE which utilizes multi-instructor data by developing an instructor coalition module that synergistically combines logits from different instructors, effectively distilling their collective knowledge into a unified dataset. Furthermore, an iterative learning module within PILE facilitates improved understanding among instructors, ultimately leading to enhanced model performance, experimentally validated on multiple datasets in three distinct learning settings, showcasing PILE's effectiveness and efficiency in handling various dataset scales and configurations. Notably, PILE achieves comparable results when trained with single-instructor data on multiple tasks, while significantly reducing training time by taking advantage of its distillation capabilities. The source code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyinliu/pile. PILE has been accepted at the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems.

We suggest a novel method called "strength interferometry" that could serve as a reliable means of detecting extremely lightweight bosonic dark matter. By cross-correlating the signals produced by two types of measurements - a high-strength elastic scattering and a low-strength Coulombic interaction - we can effectively distinguish dark matter signals from background noise. Through this technique, we've demonstrated the capability to detect a bosonic dark matter candidate with masses as low as $10^{-20}$ eV, even when faced with significant background noise from thermal fluctuations. Since the method relies on systematics-free signal analysis, it has the potential to be applied across a wide range of experimental settings, including those that use crystals, liquids, and gases as targets. We've also extended the method to simultaneously derive the dark matter mass and coupling constant. Furthermore, we've explored the application of strength interferometry in enhancing direct detection experiments that use superconducting nanograins and superfluid helium as targets, and have identified a feasible path to detect a bosonic dark matter candidate with masses as low as $10^{-22}$ eV. We've also analyzed the direct applicability of strength interferometry in monolayer kryptons and light liquids, and have found that it can detect a bosonic dark matter candidate with masses as low as $10^{-19}$ eV. This research explores the uniqueness of solutions to the basis pursuit problem within a continuous setting, and our findings reveal that under specific conditions, such as a convex transform and compact basis sets, uniqueness is certain, and this result extends to sparse recovery within Euclidean spaces under additional constraints. Furthermore, we derive precise metrics governing continuity and $\ell_1$-stability, which significantly simplify previous complex formulas, and we discuss their implications for approximate solution validity, even in the presence of noise. At the theoretical level, we address hessian continuity, establishing that the basis change matrix $\beta$ possesses positive hessian continuity if, and only if, its determinant remains consistently greater than zero throughout its domain. To demonstrate the practical utility of these metrics, we provide a detailed example illustrating how they can be employed to analyze the continuous basis pursuit problem's performance under the action of an anisotropic diffusion process. In contrast to the discrete case, where numerous stability results already exist, this study fills a gap in the existing literature by addressing the topic in the continuous domain. Additionally, the research delves into the sparsity-inducing potential of the Moreau-envelope of the $\ell_1$-norm, $\ell_p$-norm, and $\ell_\infty$-norm, and through rigorous analysis, we establish its relation to the pth power of the Euclidean norm, thereby establishing a continuous generalization of the I1, I2, and I infinity methods. Furthermore, we discuss the application of these potential functions in minimizing the Fréchet means distance between probability measures, and we derive the geometric and analytic properties of the resulting Fréchet means minimizer, thereby extending the discrete "equal spacing" theorem to the continuous domain. P4 has become the dominant choice for programming network functions due to its strong type system, table-driven architecture, and flexibility in implementing complex control logic. However, the traditional von Neumann architecture of P4 programs, with separate control and data paths, can lead to performance issues when dealing with high throughput traffic. Furthermore, modern datacenter networks require rapid hardware-driven forwarding, which can be challenging to achieve with P4 programs. To address these limitations, we developed COMPO, an open-source P4 compiler framework that enables compile-time configuration of P4 programs for hardware-driven forwarding. Our approach focuses on modifying P4 programs to conform to hardware requirements, utilizing both eternally persistent and non-persistent registers in P4. Through experiments, COMPO demonstrated the potential to facilitate hardware-driven forwarding with significant improvements, even within existing P4 programs. Details about COMPO and our findings can be found at https://tinyurl.com/Compopen-SECONIXXIX. We developed a novel approach to evaluate the performance of parallel processing in complex neural networks, allowing for efficient training on high-performance computing clusters with multiple GPUs. Our method, regional evaluator training, is a fully distributed learning technique that gives each node in the computation grid more control over the learning process. Experimental results show that regional evaluator training can accelerate the training process by up to 30% compared to traditional methods using multiple GPUs in large-scale computation grids with 64-128 GPUs. Additionally, we achieved significant reductions in memory usage during training, allowing for the development of more complex neural networks on high-performance computing clusters with multiple GPUs. Our findings also highlight the importance of considering the structure of the neural network and the distribution of its components when designing parallel processing algorithms to optimize the learning process. Our open-source code is available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. Here, Wada points are locations where three basins of attraction meet, forming a singular point. Increasing dissipation past this threshold results in Wada basins shrinking and ultimately disappearing as the area where attractions converge degenerates. It's found that extremely low levels of energy typically facilitate three-dimensional scattering, enhancing Wada features in the process. This is contrary to earlier findings from two-dimensional studies, which indicated that extremely low energy levels might result in featureless patterns within closed areas. A model was developed using a heavy object attached to an oscillating plane to visually represent this scenario, and subsequent analysis involved examining energy levels and times of passage as key variables to characterise Wada basins and understand the dynamics of this system. This work provides a foundation for future studies on the effects of energy levels on Wada basins in complex systems. It also opens doors for potential applications in areas like non-linear optics and quantum physics, where researchers might find analogous patterns and processes. Long-form activity recognition has achieved significant success through the application of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), with various methods being developed over the years to enhance performance. In contrast, recognizing activities within short video clips remains an underinvestigated area. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Hierarchical Focus Network (HFN), an end-to-end framework designed for activity recognition in short clips. In essence, the HFN leverages I3D and MultiPathNet models in a multi-stage process, with the former focused on global activity features and the latter concentrating on local details, with both stages working in tandem to extract essential information from video data. To complement the HFN, we also introduce the Focus dataset, consisting of action clips extracted from various movies and amounting to 100,000 samples. Through extensive evaluations using the Focus dataset, the HFN demonstrates superior performance when compared to alternative methods, with our model achieving an impressive accuracy of 63.3% on the FocusAction challenge's test set. Notably, the Focus dataset and HFN can be adapted for use in other action recognition applications, such as the UCF101 and Sports-1M datasets. Details regarding the implementation, dataset, and corresponding code can be found at https://github.com/zhkcos/hfn. Additionally, the Focus dataset's web interface can be accessed at http://actionclip.org. With the HFN and Focus dataset in place, we hope to stimulate further research in activity recognition for short clips. This paper proposes a new method of estimating thermal states and entropy in complex quantum many-body systems. We utilize a thermodynamic Bethe ansatz solution, but our approach can be generalized to other methods of finding thermal states. The challenge posed by the loss of dimensionality in thermal mixtures is addressed through adoption of the nested sampling technique, originally developed in the context of Bayesian inference. This incorporation enables us to estimate the partition function, crucial in thermodynamics, as well as specific heat and other thermal properties at any desired temperature. Our calculations are exemplified by examining the thermal behavior of the Heisenberg spin chain, where we find notable discrepancies between our results and existing analytical findings on the long-range scaling of entropy. Additionally, we apply our approach to determine the entanglement entropy in sub-thermal states of the XXZ chain, yielding estimates that align with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we outline potential adaptations for using nested sampling within the framework of quantum tensor networks, offering a promising avenue for studying thermal systems within the context of compact representations. Overall, our method demonstrates strong potential for accurately calculating thermal properties in complex systems, especially when analytical tools are unavailable. At the same time, we recognize that some properties may remain inherently stochastic due to the inherent randomness introduced by nested sampling at low occupancies. As such, we advocate for presenting uncertainty estimates in conjunction with our calculated values. These estimates can be obtained using techniques like bootstrapping, enabling us to gauge the precision of our findings. This level of transparency is particularly important when working with nested sampling, where the trade-offs between computational resources and precision can be particularly acute. By adopting this approach, we can ensure that the method's significant advantages in estimating thermal properties are complemented by a corresponding commitment to transparent assessments of uncertainty. This combined strategy can serve as a guiding principle for nested sampling applications in computational many-body physics. At the very least, it is our hope that this methodology will facilitate a more accurate estimation of errors in thermal properties. This large group of solutions includes not only classical solutions but also Measure-valued solutions. We identify a subset of these solutions, which we call feeble solutions, and establish that they satisfy the original partial differential equation in a modified context. This feeble solution is essentially a limiting case for a group of related bounded variation solutions as their differences become negligible. It is worth noting that feeble solutions serve as limits for a group of related bounded variation solutions as their differences vanish and, in contrast to classical solutions, they do not necessarily have the same level of smoothness. This research introduces NBcoded, an innovative network intrusion detection system tailored for resource-constrained IoT devices. NBcoded leverages a custom, two-stage classification approach involving a feature compression algorithm and a Naive Bayes/Encoder combination. During training, NBcoded compresses features using Naive Bayes to create a compact binary representation, which is then classified using an Encoder-based classifier. At runtime, an Naive Bayes classifier utilizing the compressed features derived from previous training generates a probability vector, which is subsequently classified by an Encoder-based model. Experimental results demonstrate that NBcoded achieves 93% accuracy, outperforming existing solutions such as Deep Packet Inspection and Feed Forward Neural Network, particularly in terms of power consumption and latency. With its ability to adapt to devices with limited CPU, memory, and bandwidth, NBcoded is poised to enhance IoT security on low-resource devices. Source code is available at https://github.com/ahmed-abdelkader/NBcoded.

Recent breakthroughs in applying information theory to physics have made the underlying physical laws redundant in some cases, where global principles derived from information theory take their place. However, it's currently unclear if these principles are consistent across all physical systems. If they're not, this could potentially allow for the creation of physical devices that can generate useful work without any initial input, which would defy the fundamental laws of thermodynamics and cause significant issues in our understanding of the world. In this study, we begin to explore the idea of identifying global physical laws by starting with an analysis of thermodynamics and non-equilibrium systems from an information-theoretic perspective. Our findings indicate that the Pareto global theory is inconsistent, but the microcanonical global theory is reliable and aligns well with the conventional microcanonical statistics seen in physical systems. Moreover, we've developed a new theoretical framework that enables us to quantify the Shannon information in any state of a system, which should be useful for further research in this area. In addition, we've introduced a novel method for generating entropy based on the concept of opportunities, which should also contribute meaningfully to ongoing research in this field. Our work lays the groundwork for a broader exploration of the global physical laws that underpin the world around us, which could potentially lead to significant breakthroughs in technology and our fundamental understanding of reality. It's also possible that these global laws may hold secrets that could be utilized to create advanced technologies, such as perpetual motion machines, if they were available. Fortunately, our analysis reveals that such possibilities do not exist. Finally, we've outlined the underlying assumptions of our analysis and identified areas where further research is needed to expand our understanding of the global physical laws that govern our universe. In the future, we envision that these laws will enable us to develop new and innovative technologies that can harness information to produce useful work. Conversely, our analysis also shows that information theory can be used to clarify and consolidate our existing knowledge of the fundamental laws of physics, which is a valuable byproduct of this research. It's also noteworthy that our analysis has led to some unexpected insights into the underlying nature of reality, which highlights the profound potential of information theory to illuminate the mysteries of physics. In the end, we've demonstrated that information theory can serve as a complementary framework to physics, providing new perspectives and insights into the global principles that govern our universe. While our analysis has identified some inconsistencies in the global physical laws, we've also shown that these principles can be relied upon to explain a wide range of phenomena in physical systems. Neutron scattering has emerged as a crucial tool for investigating the dynamics of light isotopic impurities within host materials. This technique is particularly effective due to the minimal disruption neutron scattering can cause to the system. We utilize neutron scattering to examine the behavior of deuterium within magnesium oxide, revealing a complex band structure consisting of shallow and deeper levels. Deeper levels exhibit slower dynamics compared to shallow levels and can form strong chemical bonds with the surrounding environment. This research demonstrates the potential for neutron scattering to study the behavior of radionuclides, providing valuable insights for nuclear medicine applications. Furthermore, the methodology employed in this study can be adapted for analyzing other materials and environmental conditions. Additionally, we discuss the possibility of utilizing other low-intensity beams, such as MEIC at JLab or LASER-SPALLATION NEUTRON SOURCE at Brookhaven, for such research. Suicidal individuals often convey their intentions through subtle hints, which can go unnoticed by others. Early detection and intervention is critical to prevent such tragedies. This research introduces a novel framework that integrates multiple data sources - clinical interviews and patient records - to accurately predict suicidal thoughts. The interview data present a sequential problem with temporal relationships, whereas the records contain vital demographic and medical history data to inform suicidal tendencies. Our framework combines a suicidal risk assessment model, which analyzes interview data, with a classifier that utilizes historical patient data to make the final prediction. The risk assessment model leverages bidirectional and attention-based LSTM architectures to capture both local and global cues, while the classifier employs a deep neural network that incorporates features extracted from the records. The outcome shows that our system significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a 0.81 AUC on predicting suicidal thoughts from sequential clinical interview data and providing valuable features for improved prediction using patient records. The study demonstrates the value of combining multiple data sources in predicting suicidal risk. The developed model is deployed as a web service, enabling clinicians to leverage electronic health records and enhance suicidal risk assessments with local context. The system is currently in use at the BWH suicide intervention team to facilitate clinical practice. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashishs97/Suicidal-Thoughts-Deep-Sequential-Framework. The dataset used in this research can be obtained from https://phoenix.brown.edu/ under the label "C-SSRQ". This work introduces a novel method to represent and study the interfaces between gas and liquid phases in two-dimensional flows using skeletal data structures. By leveraging the principles of Voronoi diagrams and Delaunay triangulations, we generate skeletons in real-time, allowing for their computation during online analysis. A graph representation, denoted as $\mathcal{G}$, is utilized to store skeleton information, which encompasses the interplay between branch points (vertices) and segments (edges). A quantitative measure, branch point importance, is defined and used to prioritize vertices during reduction operations, resulting in a simplified representation of the interface. This method enhances online analysis capabilities by providing a compact representation of the interface and enabling calculations with reduced complexity. It is demonstrated that the proposed approach outperforms traditional interface representations in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy, as evidenced by its ability to accurately track the interface area and gross error for various flow types, even at high speeds. Furthermore, the method enables the computation of the Stokes stress tensor and the Reynolds stress tensor at specified points, as shown in the presented results. A Python package, pySkeleton, is developed to implement this method and is made available for public use. The method's efficacy is validated through experiments on three multi-phase flow types: a single bubble rising due to surface tension, a collision between two droplets, and a periodic flow with oscillating bubbles. The detailed implementation and analysis of this method can be found in the accompanying open-source repository at https://github.com/NeSTMLG/pySkeleton. A Jupyter notebook is also provided for online visualization at https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/gist/ahmedebrahim/7a5f0b8c0c0e4b5c5a0c0100c. First, we adapt a established semantics from Spreafico and Moggi, converting it into a more refined version with improved properties; 
Second, we develop a semantics from a probabilistic extension of Kleene's semantics by Kozen; 
Both initial semantics are enhanced to reflect the calculus's probabilistic nature, then shown to be soundly related to each other. 
The probabilistic nature is captured by using closed probability distributions on terms, rather than traditional notions of equality or approximation, which can be misleading in probabilistic contexts. 
Instead, we define a preorder and useful notions of approximation and equality, demonstrating cut-elimination provides a strong form of equivalence that extends to probabilistic contexts. 
We also examine how the calculus interacts with probabilities through integration of measures, showing how the calculus's structure naturally relates to concepts in domain theory and topology. 
Finally, we provide a simple example to illustrate the difference in understanding the calculus with and without a probabilistic focus. 
The work presented here is part of the author's doctoral research at the University of Bath.

To identify these decays, researchers used hadronic second particles of recoil $B$ meson from $B^+$ decays into various final states. To calculate signal and background rates, researchers employed a maximum likelihood method. As a result, we obtained branching fractions for $B^0$ decays into $\rho^-\pi^+$ and $\rho^- \jot{\rho}$ with lepton flavors $\ell = e$ or $\mu$, which correspond to $4.23 \pm 0.50 (stat.) \pm 0.24 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$ and $3.04 \pm 0.34 (stat.) \pm 0.17 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$ respectively. This study presents a novel deep generative architecture that overcomes this limitation by allowing training on a separate domain of available data. This model utilizes two latent spaces - one for the source domain and one for the target domain - and incorporates an encoder to translate between the two domains. Through a series of experiments involving visual manipulation and domain translation, we demonstrate that our method excels in creating realistic synthetic data and outperforms existing models. Additionally, we apply our model to generate novel images by mimicking the styles of famous artists. Our model's code will be publicly available.

The data mining approach known as association rule mining has become a standard tool in data analysis.  The method measures consumer behavior based on sales transaction data and is widely used to guide business decisions.  This approach creates multiple rules for each transaction, leading to a vast number of rules some of which may be unnecessary, rendering them unhelpful for decision-making purposes.  Researchers have proposed several methods to reduce the number of rules, focusing on eliminating confidence and support requirements.  This study examines an alternative method that aims to eliminate rule redundancy, defining redundant rules as those inferable from other rules.  The study introduces a metric for inferring schemes and uses this metric to identify a minimal-size base for association rules, providing a strategy to reduce rule redundancy.  The proposed strategy outperforms existing methods in retaining a relevant number of rules and minimizing inference complexity.  The results of experiments using public datasets validate the effectiveness of the strategy.  Additionally, the study presents a method to reduce redundancy in rules without minimum confidence and support requirements.  The study's findings are consistent with expectations, showing that retaining more confident rules leads to fewer rules with less confidence and vice versa.  The research also presents an open-source implementation of the approach called RedBase.  The study evaluates RedBase using 24 public datasets and compares its performance to other reduction methods, showing that it retains relevant rules with minimal inference and achieves faster inference times.  The study concludes by highlighting potential applications of the approach, such as reducing noise in rule sets and facilitating the deployment of rule-based models in resource-constrained devices.  The research also suggests several avenues for future research, including the extension of the approach to other data mining techniques and the application of the approach to other domains. This research presents a novel approach to fault identification based on the responsibility of hidden Markov models (HMMs) in predicting abnormalities. When an HMM indicates anomalies, it suggests the model's initial state is not responsible, implying the abnormality arises from discrepancies in gauge probability. To address this issue, we have developed a method to optimize abnormal detection by adjusting the gauge probability of HMMs. First, we cluster similar state transitions within the same HMM model or separate HMM models. Then, we analyze the frequency of state transitions and create a transition graph to define a new form of responsibility, known as gauge probability. Finally, we test our approach in two real-world scenarios, including predicting student behavior to customize learning suggestions and detecting abnormal medical readings using electronic health records. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in identifying abnormalities. Currently, digital assistants like Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant rely on pre-prepared response templates to adapt to user queries with unknown words. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach that leverages raw audio input to improve their understanding and response. Our method involves generating speaker-specific audio components for predefined vocabulary, allowing us to create customized reactions to queries containing unknown words. To achieve this efficiently, we developed a minimally intrusive training process that enhances existing models with data augmentation capabilities. Our results show that this approach results in more natural and accurate interactions with minimal computational overhead. Specifically, our method achieves a significant improvement of 8.8% over baseline systems in terms of accuracy, while also reducing response times by up to 29ms.
