Building on previous research, our study addresses the challenge of maintaining data confidentiality in datasets that contain interdependent data attributes. Although one-sided differential privacy shows promise in this area, it has yet to be thoroughly evaluated. In this research, we first assess the effectiveness of one-sided differential privacy under strict conditions and reveal that it falls short in real-world applications. Next, we introduce a novel dependence measure between data characteristics, which can be utilized to determine the severity of data breaches. A data breach is defined as an event in which an attacker gains access to sensitive information regarding a data subject's multiple characteristics. We develop two innovative algorithms to prevent data breaches within dependent characteristics, one-sided differential privacy and the fractional transformation method. Compared to the fractional transformation, our proposed algorithm significantly enhances privacy while maintaining comparable utility. Our findings are substantiated through experiments conducted on various datasets. Our study provides a framework for evaluating data confidentiality in datasets containing interdependent data attributes, which can aid researchers and practitioners in their efforts to protect sensitive data. Additionally, our two designed algorithms offer practical solutions to prevent data breaches resulting from data subjects' multiple characteristics. These contributions can be utilized to inform theoretical research and practical applications in data confidentiality protection. The formation of planets is intricately linked with the characteristics of the surrounding protoplanetary disk, specifically its volatile distribution. The latest observations of the AS 209 disk by MAPS reveal CO depletion at specific velocities, potentially indicating the disk's volatile evolution. By combining spatial and velocity maps, we analyze CO's spatial distribution at various velocities. At velocities of -1 to -0.1 km/s, CO is significantly depleted, whereas at velocities of -0.4 to -0.1 km/s, CO is undetected and replaced by C18O. This replacement is likely a result of photochemical processing rather than physical destruction. To further understand CO depletion, we compared observations with theoretical models, focusing on the radial distribution of the disk's mass and dust. The resulting models reveal that CO depletion is primarily driven by the interaction between the disk and its parent star, specifically in regions where the disk's mass and distance from the star are closely tied. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of radiative transfer and photochemistry in shaping the disk's volatile distribution, setting the stage for future planetary formation studies. The concept of gentle solutions builds upon the average field games of controls with no state constraints, first explored by Cardaliaguet, Samson, and Tardos in 2018. The proof utilizes an iterative method that converges towards a solution, relying on estimates that can be calculated without resorting to classical $L^1$ convergence, instead utilizing a metric space framework focused on the Lipschitz norm and its relation to the Wasserstein distance. The approach allows for the inclusion of state limits as constraints, expanding the applicable class to include controls with state limits, defined by a combination of differential equations and inequality conditions. The application of the Wasserstein distance and the metric space framework facilitated a more streamlined proof, reducing the complexity of prior research. The concept and methods provide a foundation for further exploration into the dynamics of these gentle solutions. The discovery of thousands of new Milky Way stellar "threads" using machine learning is presented, along with a comprehensive analysis of their properties and patterns. Through detailed examination, it is revealed that the majority of these threads are composed of multiple distinct stars, often with similar characteristics, which can be identified using a simple machine-learning algorithm. The findings suggest that the distribution of thread lengths in the Galaxy is best explained by a uniform model, and that the threads are predominantly composed of stars younger than 3 Gyr, with metallicities ranging from -1.00 to -0.50, and averaging around -0.65. The data also indicate that the threads are rotating faster than would be expected based on their location in the Galaxy. The origin of these threads is attributed to the disruption of open clusters by dynamical forces, and further research is recommended to determine the rate at which these clusters are destroyed. The goal of Visual Inconsistency Detection (VID) is to identify discrepancies in an online shopping product image display sequence that does not accurately reflect a single item's attributes.  Given a product's complex visual characteristics and the likelihood of inaccurate representations resulting from variations in lighting and pose, developing a robust VID method presents a significant challenge.  To tackle this issue, we introduce the Visual Inconsistency Detection with Transformers (VICTOR) model, which leverages a custom-designed multi-scale feature fusion approach and an optimized scoring system.  To enhance VICTOR's performance, we also propose the Fashion-oriented ViLT (FOViLT) contrastive pre-training framework, which pre-trains a model on a vast dataset of fashion product images.  The FOViLT framework yields a notable improvement in VID accuracy and surpasses the performance of leading transformer-based image recognition models when applied to the in-store product image transformation scenario.  In experiments, VICTOR achieved a 77.6% accuracy on the Fashion-VID dataset, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.  Furthermore, pre-training on the FashionNet dataset obtained a 79.1% accuracy, exceeding the baseline model's performance by 6.3%. focusing on a particular implementation known as Federated Learning (FL). We 
investigate how asynchronous communication in FL can result in performance issues 
stemming from inconsistent and outdated gradient information shared among workers. 
To mitigate these effects, we introduce a new aggregation technique called BSA, 
which incorporates the average gradient from each worker within a buffer before 
sharing it with the server. This approach, building on existing BAGD and PS methods, 
improves FL's stability and accuracy in high-communication-cost scenarios, even 
when worker synchronization with the server is delayed. We demonstrate that 
BSA's benefits arise from two key factors: the elimination of performance drops due 
to communication disruptions and the reduction of weight updates following 
communication resumption. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions under which 
BSA outperforms current FL implementations in a variety of practical applications, 
even when communication disruptions are minimal. We also release open-source code 
for replicating our experiments. We anticipate that BSA will contribute to the

unintended consequence of the current gradient aggregation practices in FL and

This study investigates how high pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. At ordinary pressure, this material exhibits an incommensurate long-range magnetic order that causes an anomalous Hall effect. When subjected to 12 GPa in pressure, this incommensurate order transforms into a hexagonal structure that lacks this phenomenon. Below 12 GPa, the two phases coexist over a 2 GPa range, allowing for the adjustment of the anomalous Hall effect through structural changes, a novel property in antiferromagnets. This study examines a Steklov-Robin type spectral problem for the Lamé system within a bounded, convex domain in n-dimensional space. We demonstrate the existence of countably infinite unique eigenvalues and associated functions, and derive asymptotic formulas for these eigenvalues. Moreover, we investigate the limits of the eigenvalues as the Robin parameter approaches zero from either the positive or negative direction. We find that these limits correspond to eigenvalues of the related Steklov problem, with multiples counting. This work is an extension of a previous study on the Laplacian by the first author. Additionally, we discuss possible generalizations of our findings to broader equations and offer an alternative proof of one of the key estimates in this paper's second chapter. To assess the dangers posed by highly viscous multiphase flows such as mudflows, we develop an estimation technique that incorporates elements of solid mechanics and the optics industry. Since these flows are difficult to predict accurately and real-time conditions make them hard to observe directly, we developed a method to estimate their risk on inclined planes using features that can be measured easily from a distance. By applying principles from Drucker-Prager plasticity and the behavior of viscous fluids in steady states, we derived a formula to calculate shear rates from features like spacing, height, and angle of layers. We tested our method using laboratory-created mudflows with varying levels of viscosity and compared the estimated values with actual measurements, finding a positive linear correlation. Additionally, we applied our technique to study real-world mudflows on two volcanic islands, further validating our approach. Textiles exhibiting repeating patterns are susceptible to defects that affect their aesthetic appeal and functionality,  thereby reducing their value.  Identifying these defects in textiles is a complex challenge,  making defect detection and classification a pressing issue in the textile industry.  Most existing methods focus on traditional knit fabrics,  overlooking the growing market for textiles with patterned designs.  This paper introduces a novel approach to detecting defects in textiles with patterned designs by utilizing the properties of gabor gradients in oriented gradients (GHOG).  This proposed method surpasses previous performance benchmarks,  outperforming other methods in detecting defects in these types of fabrics.  Additionally,  we address the issue of defective textile data classification,  given the limited availability of data,  by employing a low-rank decomposition strategy.  This approach allows us to generate synthetic data from existing samples,  thus enhancing our training capabilities.  To validate the efficacy of our proposed method,  we created a comprehensive dataset consisting of 10 distinct textile patterns,  totaling 5000 images,  and varying levels of defects.  Our findings indicate that our method successfully identifies defects in these textures and demonstrates classification accuracy on our custom dataset.  Furthermore,  we successfully applied our proposed method to real-world textile defect classification scenarios.  This research has been publicly shared through https://github.com/TextileDefectECIT/TextileDefectClassification,  enabling others to access the code and dataset.  To evaluate our method's robustness,  we employed various metrics such as precision,  recall,  F1-score,  mean IU,  and mean pixel accuracy.  Our approach,  centered around ghog and low-rank decomposition,  yields superior results,  surpassing other state-of-the-art techniques.  Specifically,  our method achieves an mIU of 0.9537,  outperforming other methods,  and achieving an accuracy of 97.57%,  along with precision and recall of 0.9703 and 0.9537 respectively.  Notably,  our approach,  and associated code,  and custom dataset,  are publicly accessible through https://github.com/TextileDefectECIT/TextileDefectClassification.  This will facilitate other researchers in replicating our findings and potentially improving upon our method.  In terms of future work,  we envision extending our method to other domains,  and exploring other techniques that leverage low-rank and gabor gradients in oriented gradients (GHOG).

To successfully conduct visual navigation in complex environments, a robot must effectively utilize information from visual observations, taking into account both state uncertainty and data reliability. Current methods, which often employ reinforcement learning, fall short in this regard, as they typically disregard the limitations of sensory data and assume optimal reliability. To address this issue, we present a new approach that leverages a data-driven framework to develop a navigation agent capable of making informed decisions in various visual scenarios. By promoting diverse exploration and striking a balance between short-term rewards and long-term consistency, our method enables a robot to navigate confidently and achieve superior performance in challenging benchmarks. Notably, our navigation agent can adapt to novel environments without further training, as it acquires a general understanding of data reliability through the agent's interactive experiences. To facilitate robust decision-making in uncertain environments, we introduce a novel regularizer that estimates sensory data reliability based on the agent's state predictions. By integrating this data-theoretic regularizer into reinforcement learning, we develop a self-supervised framework for view prediction, which enables a robot to assess the credibility of sensory observations and navigate accordingly. As a result, our method achieves a 12.5% relative improvement in success rates compared to the leading approaches in the NYU-V2D dataset, which simulates indoor visual navigation. Moreover, our method exhibits superior robustness against adversarial manipulations of sensory data, as it effectively utilizes information from multiple sources to navigate and achieves a 30.6% relative improvement in success rates compared to the leading approaches in the RoboAI-Sim dataset, which simulates outdoor visual navigation. Real-time monitoring of power distribution networks (PDN) enables efficient control over the infrastructure, however, current methods relying on sophisticated sensor equipment are impractical for widespread use due to high costs. An alternative approach using historical smart meter data and data mining techniques could provide a more feasible solution, albeit with limited effectiveness due to the reliance on event recurrence for detection. This research introduces an enhanced data-driven event identification method in PDN, combining statistical and machine learning strategies to optimize performance, and evaluates its effectiveness through comparative analysis with a previous proposed algorithm, as well as two popular approaches in the field. The findings indicate that this method can achieve promising results, with an accuracy rate of 80% and a false positive rate of 10%, for a general PDN scenario. Moreover, the analysis suggests that the method's performance can be fine-tuned to accommodate specific event characteristics and requirements, thereby enabling adaptation to various PDN applications. An estimated reduction in false positives of 60% is achievable in scenarios where prior knowledge of fault patterns exists. This proposed method has the potential to contribute to the development of more cost-effective and scalable real-time PDN monitoring systems. Experimental validation of the method's efficacy using actual data from the University of Alberta's distribution network is also presented. The corresponding source code for this research has been made available on GitHub for public access. Furthermore, the results of the study, including the data, can be found on OpenScience, enabling reproduction of the findings by the research community. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess the capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) to navigate intricate, dynamic environments through command-line interactions. The text-based game benchmark, used in the 2018 Text-Based Game AI Challenge, has been widely employed in AI research due to its simple interface and capacity to model complex environments. However, this benchmark's limitations become apparent when processing the game data, as it requires converting text inputs into numerical representations using one-hot encoding or similar methods, and then performing lookup operations during the game simulation. These processes can impede the game's speed by as much as 300 times. To address this issue, we developed TextWorldExpress, an optimized open-source platform for simulating text-based games at an unprecedented speed of one million moves per second on standard hardware. TextWorldExpress achieves this remarkable speed through several groundbreaking innovations: it utilizes a custom-built hash table for rapid environment updates, a compact numerical representation of game objects, and a low-overhead data structure for quickly retrieving and modifying game entities. Additionally, TextWorldExpress incorporates a novel, highly efficient data format for storing game levels and includes a range of tools for easily creating new game levels and modifying existing ones. We validated TextWorldExpress's performance by comparing it to the original text-based game benchmark and observed a remarkable 180,000-fold speed increase. Furthermore, we used TextWorldExpress to simulate extensive game sessions lasting several days, thereby generating vast amounts of data, and then employed reinforcement learning to develop efficient game-solving strategies from this data. Our research demonstrates the significant performance benefits that can be achieved through game-benchmark optimization and highlights the vast potential of text-based games in AI research, as evidenced by the 1 million moves-per-second speed at which TextWorldExpress can simulate these games. To study Higgs boson pairs produced through the process $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ at the LHC using the ATLAS and CMS experiments' detector level data, a novel approach is proposed. This approach involves employing the matrix element technique in conjunction with two distinct reconstruction methods for the Higgs bosons. Firstly, a traditional reconstruction method utilizing the Higgs boson's decay into bottom quarks and electrons or muons from the other experiment is used. A common requirement in robotics and computer vision is to estimate the 3D position and orientation of an object. Traditionally, this task relies on labeled data, but in this research, a model is developed that can predict 3D pose from video footage showing an object rotating unintentionally. The study focuses on turntables as objects and proposes the Turntable Dataset with 12 turntables featuring over 5000 poses in RGB and depth formats. The dataset also includes a challenge to extract 3D pose from video footage automatically. The proposed model, RTBNet, uses a two-stage process to predict 3D pose by initially estimating the rotation matrix and then using so-called "3D distance" to refine the outcome. When tested on the new dataset, RTBNet outperforms other models, demonstrating its ability to generalize to various scenarios. The study showcases the potential for new applications with the dataset, such as automatically generating 3D models and identifying turntables in real-world environments. Recently, social media platforms have become a primary source of information for many people. Unfortunately, this has led to the dissemination of false information through these platforms, which poses a significant threat to public health. In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, a novel approach to tackling this issue is presented. This involves using machine learning to detect the spread of false information about COVID-19 vaccines within online conversations. By defining the terms acceptance and refusal as retweeting or replying to pro-uncertainty messages, a dataset was created from Twitter dialogue and tested against various classifiers using BERT and multi-layer perceptrons. The findings indicate that BERT outperformed traditional machine learning methods and multi-task models by 9% and 4% respectively in predicting user responses. Furthermore, the research found that users who initially accepted pro-uncertainty messages were more likely to be classified as refusals after being exposed to counterarguments. In contrast, initial refusals remained largely unchanged. In addition to identifying acceptance and refusal, the research also developed a new metric called net response, which quantifies the shift in user attitudes toward pro-uncertainty messages over time. In experiments using this net response metric, it was found that users who initially responded negatively to pro-uncertainty messages became more accepting than those who initially responded positively. The proposed approach effectively models the dynamic interactions between pro-uncertainty messages and their corresponding counterarguments, as well as the varying responses of users to these messages over time. In the future, this research can be applied to other online platforms beyond Twitter and used to inform the development of automated systems capable of mitigating the spread of false information online. In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, the presented work can be utilized to create personalized recommendations for users who have been exposed to pro-uncertainty messages, advising them on relevant information sources that can help alleviate their vaccine-related concerns. In the longer term, this research can contribute to the development of a machine learning-based system capable of automatically addressing user concerns and promoting the spread of accurate information about COVID-19 vaccines. Our research identified three previously unrecognized low-mass companions associated with the Algol system, specifically located in the vicinity of its bright inner binary star, the eclipsing pair known as the A and B components.  By analyzing archival images from the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System, we discovered three faint companions, designated as C, D, and E, with estimated masses ranging from 0.1 to 0.3 times that of the Sun.  By modeling their orbital paths, we calculated the system's parameters and found that the orbital plane of these companions aligns closely with that of the A and B binary stars.  With the C companion's 20-year orbital period serving as a temporal marker, we were able to reevaluate past observations of the system, including those from the 19th and 20th centuries, and discovered potential references to it.  By incorporating the C companion's orbital motion into the system's long-term dynamics, we found that it may have originated from a circumbinary disk that formed alongside the Algol stars.  The presence of these companions challenges the conventional understanding of the system's evolution, which had been thought to be restricted to binary systems.  Instead, the emergence of these companions from a circumbinary disk suggests that run-away planetary formation may be a more widespread phenomenon than previously believed, even affecting inner regions close to the star.  Further research using next-generation telescopes, such as the Giant Ultralight Telescope, is needed to determine the mass, size, and orbital characteristics of the D and E companions, as well as to assess the possibility of a circumbinary disk still present in the system today.  The discovery of these companions also raises questions about the system's dynamical past, including the potential role of external gravitational disturbances in shaping its evolution, and whether the eclipsing binary star Algol may have been formed through a distinct mechanism, such as the secular mean motion resonance, rather than via a stellar encounter.  The fresh perspectives offered by our research highlight the need for ongoing observational efforts to reexamine the dynamical history of this iconic system and its many secrets, particularly its past dynamical evolution, which remains poorly understood, remain to be uncovered.

The freight network is an intricate system influenced by diverse factors, 
including external elements like weather, transportation modes, shippers, and receivers.
This research aims to investigate the resilience of freight systems to various disruptions.
A novel methodology has been devised to create an Dependency-Fragility Insight Graph (DFIG) 
for freight networks, allowing for the measurement of sensitivity to disruptions.
Case studies are employed to demonstrate the method's effectiveness and compare the resilience of different freight networks. 
Notably, the proposed approach can be applied beyond freight to other supply chain management contexts.

The graph's nodes encompass freight network entities (shippers, receivers, carriers, modes of transportation), 
along with external factors (weather, etc.), which are interconnected according to their relative importance.
A directed edge from entity A to entity B exists if A's disruption affects B's performance.
Each entity's fragility score represents its vulnerability to disruptions.
This research presents two methods for determining these scores: one based on relative impact and another based on spread. 
The relative impact method calculates fragility through the comparison of each entity's relative importance and disruption spread.
On the other hand, the spread method employs the PageRank algorithm to determine disruption spread and then calculates fragility through the comparison of each entity's relative importance and disruption spread.
By combining these metrics, the DFIG provides a comprehensive understanding of freight ecosystem behavior under disruptions.
This research applies the DFIG to study the resilience of two freight networks: one representing air cargo and another representing intermodal freight.
The results show that the air cargo network is more resilient than the intermodal network.
Furthermore, the approach can identify weak links in the freight ecosystem.
The methodology is expected to contribute positively to freight ecosystem management and planning.

This article investigates the minimum degree of the power graph associated with finite nilpotent groups, providing specific lower bounds in that context. Furthermore, we establish a minimum degree for the power graphs of certain classes of nilpotent groups: Abelian groups of a given prime factorization and groups of a given nilpotency degree. To support our findings, we also present some illustrative examples. Interestingly, for finite nilpotent groups more broadly, we discovered that the power graph's degree can be as low as $\varphi(2)$, where $\varphi$ denotes the Euler's totient function. This research was motivated in part by a question initially posed by Roberto Roldan in 2019. Additionally, we have made available on our website the source code for computers to determine the power graphs of various groups as requested in that question. Using these power graphs, computers can easily calculate the power graphs' degrees. We utilized these calculations to validate our conclusions through experimental evidence. Specifically, we have provided on our website the power graphs for groups of orders $p^2$, $p^3$, $pq$ and $p^2q$, which can serve as useful references for other researchers. Moreover, we have included on our website a written description of our research's underlying goals, along with the specific questions we aim to answer. The SHINE project aims to address key questions in cosmic ray research by leveraging the detection of secondary cosmic particles influenced by magnetic fields. To achieve this, the SHINE experiment will establish ground-based observatories tracking hadronic cosmic particles over an expansive area of more than 100,000 square meters in the Pamir region near the JINR's Dubna base. To facilitate precise analysis of the particles' properties, the SHINE team is developing an advanced spectrometer featuring cutting-edge calorimetry technology, an innovative magnetic system, and sophisticated plastic track detectors. This comprehensive spectrometer will be showcased in an exposé during the 36th International Cosmic-ray Conference in Madrid, Spain. The presentation will detail the design's underlying philosophy, the technical specifics with regard to detector integration, and the anticipated results from the first phase of SHINE's implementation, which includes the deployment of a limited version of the apparatus in Tunka, Russia. The Tunka-Shine setup will serve as a crucial stepping stone for the main SHINE experiment to come. The Tunka-Shine setup will focus on studying energy spectra, mass fractions, and other characteristics of hadronic cosmic particles, while also exploring novel methods to identify the GZK-cutoff and other key features in extensive air showers. To complement its research into cosmic particles, the SHINE team is also developing an inelasticity distribution analyzer that utilizes the Pamir scintillation detectors in tandem with the Tunka Cherenkov telescopes to investigate particle composition and new physics phenomena in extensive air showers. The SHINE project is poised to significantly advance our understanding of cosmic ray research and we are eager to embark on this scientific journey. The detailed technical details and results from the first phase of SHINE's implementation will be presented in the following sections. The SHINE project is a collaborative effort between researchers from the JINR Dubna, the Pamir State University, and the Tunka NMSU consortium. The emergence of deep learning techniques has greatly impacted point cloud processing in past years, with Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) standing out as a prominent representation learning method due to their ability to effectively learn from spatially-related point cloud data. However, traditional GCNs developed for image recognition face challenges when directly applied to point clouds due to their limited ability to capture local geometry features. To address this, a novel graph convolutional network called EGCN is proposed, designed specifically for point cloud processing and built upon an anisotropic geometric transformation. By integrating this transformation into the graph filters, EGCN enables the learning of sensitive geometric features at various orientations within point cloud data. To further optimize data preparation for the network, a novel framework called Oriented Triangular Mesh Generation (OTMG) is introduced to enhance the quality of point cloud data. By replacing traditional KNN-based neighboring selection with OTMG-generated meshes, the proposed EGCN achieves superior performance in classification and semantic segmentation tasks, outshining existing state-of-the-art methods by significant margins when evaluated using widely-used metrics on three benchmark datasets. Recently, hosted backdoors in neural networks have become a significant threat due to their undetectability. In normal operations, the host application remains legitimate, but triggers a function to stealthily manipulate inputs at prediction time. Most current methods to detect hosted backdoors assume that the host intends to execute a legitimate task, but this is impractical given the host could be an advertisement on a website with the backdoor activated through user input, indicating a critical limitation. 

This study introduces a more complex scheme called SHTA (Semantic Hostless Trojan Assault), comprising two core components - a Trojan module and a trigger mechanism. The Trojan module encodes the backdoor's operation, while the trigger is set to respond under a specific condition defined by the host. We demonstrate that traditional hosted backdoor detection methods fail in SHTA scenarios, but also observe that attempting to rectify the model's outputs alone is insufficient to eliminate the backdoor. 

To address this issue, we propose an innovative method called Hostless Clean-Natural-Training (HCTN), which separates the detection of the host from the correction of the model's outputs. The host can be detected using a semantic analysis based on the input data's semantic features to define the backdoor's activation condition, and subsequently corrected through a supervised learning process. Our experiments show that HCTN successfully detects and eliminates hosted backdoors under real-world conditions, outperforming existing methods. We employed the Magellan IMACS spectrograph at the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Telescope network to establish a robust, on-the-fly, 2D spectrographic system, referred to as the ROSIE-2 integral field unit. This system was based on the original ROSIE IFU, which we initially set up in 2013, with the primary goal of utilizing it for globular cluster studies at the Magellan Baade Telescope. However, due to the telescope's maintenance, we transitioned the system to the Magellan II Deeprak reflector and enhanced it with two e2V 2400 grisms, along with a 0.6x Magellan II demagnifier to optimize our field of view. This upgrade resulted in a 4.5' by 1.1" field of view at a 0.86 arcsecond/pixel resolution. Our tests with a 1024x1024 CCD demonstrated the capability to collect 10-module full spectra in approximately 13.2 seconds. This system's enhanced features and optimized settings make ROSIE-2 an advanced and efficient tool for a wide range of astronomical observations. Our findings demonstrate that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{cat}}$ is a subalgebra of the reduced algebra, $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$, where $\mathcal{H}$ is the reduced tensor product of $L^2(G)$ with itself. Our work also addresses the dual scenario, where we examine the functions, $\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cat}}$, associated with the dual compact quantum group, $(G^*,\Delta^*)$, and establish similar results. Computer experiments, where the outcome is measured over time, are frequently hindered by the high computational cost involved in running them multiple times. To make these experiments more feasible, we treat the trajectory of each run as a time series and reduce it to a key summary using the Multi-Contour Assessment method. This representation enables us to apply traditional classification techniques in a lower-dimensional space, where similarities in time series can be captured. Our approach is adaptable to various types of time series modifications and can incorporate uncertainties directly into the results. Moreover, it doesn't require us to assume a specific distribution for the errors and allows for the inclusion of costs associated with different prediction errors. To assess the effectiveness of this approach, we conduct a thorough evaluation using 24 real-world applications from diverse fields, which demonstrates that our method excels at accurately representing the trajectory of each run and identifying the best options within a reasonable time frame. Furthermore, it is also an efficient scalable solution. You can find the implementation details and the used data on our website. Recent research revealed a peculiar object, designated WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, 
initially classified as a low-mass brown dwarf based on its spectral characteristics.
However, its luminosity appears to defy expectations, prompting a reevaluation 
of its nature. To better comprehend this enigma, we conducted a follow-up study 
utilizing spectroscopy and atmospheric modeling. Our analysis, coupled with parallax 
measurement, suggests that the object's spectral energy distribution is distorted 
by significant dust obscuration. By modeling its atmosphere, we identified 
moleculary-cooled dust within its atmosphere as the primary contributor to this 
distortion. Our findings imply that the object's apparent temperature and 
luminosity are artificially inflated due to the effects of dust. With corrected 
parallax measurement of 123.8 +/- 3.3 microarcseconds, the object's true nature 
becomes apparent, with a mass of approximately 0.075 Msun falling within the 
range of extremely low-mass objects. By examining the object's demographics, 
we note that its characteristics are not isolated and propose that such objects may 
be more prevalent than initially thought, with potential implications for the 
definition of the brown dwarf planetary boundary. Further research using larger 
telescopes is recommended to investigate the object's magnetic field and 
binarity status, which could shed more light on its unique properties. If these 
objects are found to be more common, it may necessitate a reevaluation of the 
definition of what constitutes a planet and a brown dwarf. Additionally, their 
existence raises questions about the accuracy of various low-mass object selection 
algorithms used in surveys and may necessitate adjustments to improve their 
detection. Lastly, their peculiar nature presents a challenge to current 
theoretical models of low-mass object formation, which may need to be revised to 
account for their observed properties. To facilitate further research, we have 
published the complete dataset used in this study, including spectra, atmospheric 
models, and other relevant data. This research aims to stimulate a more in-depth 
investigation of these enigmatic objects, which could lead to new insights into the 
formation of low-mass objects in our solar neighborhood. To access the data, 
please visit the DOI: 10.7910/DVN/3JQ9MZ. This research was supported by the National

This approach necessitates the development of PDFs for vector and axial components of reggeized quarks, which we call $S$ and $P$ distribution functions. To efficiently obtain these functions, we adapt an effective progression operator used in neural network research and demonstrate its suitability with virtual neutrino interactions at 13 TeV for the $S$ distribution functions, resulting in significantly reduced computation time compared to other methods. Additionally, we successfully apply this operator to $P$ distribution functions through duality. Our research also highlights the importance of considering $P$ distribution functions in parton-based analysis, particularly when working with low-x data. This work includes the definition of $S$ and $P$ distribution functions, the testing of reggeized quark properties, and the exploration of parton-based color components in the context of reggeized quarks. Our research also includes the prediction of relevant cross-sections influenced by $P$ distribution functions for double-diffractive collisions at 13 TeV. We conducted a study on the reliability of star formation rates derived from SED fitting using a sample of 274 star-forming galaxies from the MaNGA survey, with a focus on the calibration against observed recombination lines. Despite using different methods for SED fitting and line emission diagnostics, we found a consistent linear relationship between the rates derived from lines and those predicted by SED fitting. However, we noticed that the predicted rates are generally lower than those derived from lines, with an average underprediction of 0.3 dex. Since predicting line emission is another key aspect of modeling galaxy evolution, we explored the possibility of using it as a feedback mechanism to improve the accuracy of SED-derived star formation rates. By incorporating line emission into the models, we found that the predicted rates have a reduced underprediction and are closer to those derived from lines. Overall, our study suggests that using recombination lines like Brackett-$\gamma$ as a benchmark can help constrain the models and improve their predictions of star formation rates. Moreover, we found that the predicted rates by using MaNGA's line data are more consistent with those from other methods, with an average dispersion of 0.1 dex, which highlights the potential of using line data as a diagnostic tool to refine the models. Our study also offers a straightforward way for future surveys to improve the accuracy of SED modeling, with the added benefit of providing more reliable rates of star formation. Finally, we note that incorporating line data into the models can reverse the direction of spectral features that would otherwise be interpreted as being too cool, which could lead to improved photometric corrections in future surveys. With the advent of future spectroscopic surveys like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time, our proposed approach can be used to further constrain the models and provide more reliable galaxy evolution rates. Based on the expected data, we predict that the predicted rates will have an average underprediction of less than 0.1 dex. With the added depth and coverage of future surveys, the predicted rates will be nearly indistinguishable from those derived from lines. In other words, our study suggests that future surveys will be deep enough to directly use SED fitting to predict reliable galaxy evolution rates, without needing to use recombination lines like Brackett-$\gamma$ as a benchmark. However, this will require including emission lines from the depth of 20 AB magnitudes in spectroscopic surveys. Without such lines, the predicted rates will have a significant underprediction of at least 0.6 dex.

This research introduces an innovative, length-synthesis approach for speech
generation entirely based on a non-mathematical method. Unlike existing techniques
that rely on probability theory, this new approach leverages median relationships
within speech to create synthetic samples of varied lengths. By circumventing the
need for statistical formulas, this non-statistical method can be easily replicated
and its efficacy demonstrated. This study first establishes the validity of its
speech length estimation method and then effectively employs it within a synthetic
speech generation process, resulting in speech samples of clearly defined, varied
 durations. Furthermore, the resulting synthetic speech exhibits characteristics
similar to its real counterpart, including its natural prosodic rhythm and speech
density. To validate its efficacy, this research presents objective metrics and
subjective listener feedback confirming the substantial effectiveness of this new,
non-statistical approach. Notably, listener preferences revealed that even experienced
translators and linguists were unable to distinguish the synthetic speech produced
by this method as originating from a real speaker. Speech samples generated using
this new non-statistical method can be accessed at https://speech-median.github.io/.

We've developed a novel two-part neural network approach to capture the temporal evolution in the spectral characteristics of Type Ia Supernovae. By employing a stochastic autoencoder, we've trained the model to learn the intrinsic variations in SN Ia spectra, which are superimposed with random noise representative of observational uncertainties. The encoder section of the network compresses the sequence of spectral samples into a single probabilistic code, while the decoder transforms this code back into spectral sample sequences. Utilizing the autoencoder, we've extracted dimensionally reduced representations of temporal sequences from the low signal-to-noise ratio spectra from the SN Ia subsample within the SDSS-III/BOSS dataset. Furthermore, we've applied our method to investigate the dependence of temporal sequences on several intrinsic parameters of SN Ia events through an analysis of their manifold structure. The results indicate that our approach holds promise for future research on SN Ia cosmology to effectively utilize low signal-to-noise ratio time sequences. Additionally, this technique can serve as a versatile tool for data reduction and feature extraction in various astronomical applications. The incorporation rate is found to be dependent on two factors: the fluid's flow velocity and the angle at which the spheres sit relative to the plume's centerline. The incorporation process is slowed when the spheres are positioned at an angle, and this effect becomes more pronounced in regions with lower fluid flow velocities and near the plume's base. In recent years, deep learning methods have gained significant attention for
addressing multimodal problems, yet current frameworks face challenges such as
model complexity, feature duplication, and difficulty in capturing domain-specific
characteristics.  To address these issues, we present a novel deep learning
framework called the K-fan Deep Framework (KDF).  This framework enables the
creation of various models from a common architecture through different parameter
configurations, allowing for efficient control and adaptation.  We also propose
a new method for shared representations using a multimodal encoder, along with
two additional techniques for enhancing performance: using a prior-based classifier
and incorporating attention mechanisms.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our
framework by applying it to two complex problems, multilabel classification and
multimodal image classification, and experimentally validate its advantages over
existing models.  Our framework offers several benefits, including a compact model
size, improved training stability, and enhanced generalization ability.  We also
conduct an ablation study to verify the contribution of each component.  Finally,
we showcase the performance of our framework in real-world applications through
experimental evaluation and analysis of its parameters.  The source code of our
framework is available for public access at https://github.com/zhaozhany/KDF.

This paper introduces McMini, a versatile tool for verifying the correctness of multithreaded programs based on DPOR, the Dynamic Predication Operation. Unlike other model checkers which often integrate a specific DPOR-based verifier directly into McMini, the paper examines two approaches of combining McMini with the DPOR-based verifier called McDPOR. One approach involves incorporating McDPOR as a built-in verifier in McMini, but with certain limitations on its use. The other approach involves generating a McDPOR-based verifier specifically tailored to the characteristics of the multithreaded program in question, but at the cost of increased computational complexity. The paper also explores the advantages and disadvantages of these two approaches, as well as their respective performance benefits. Finally, the paper highlights McDPOR's potential to improve McMini's capabilities in handling complex, multi-staged programs that involve side effects like memory allocation. However, this potential comes with a trade-off in increased computational complexity. The full McDPOR-based McMini implementation is accessible via https://mcmini.github.io/McDPOR. The McDPOR tool is currently compatible with McMini version 2.0 and later. The paper also includes comprehensive experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of McDPOR in verifying a diverse range of multithreaded programs, as well as its potential to improve McMini's performance in certain scenarios. The McDPOR-based McMini tool has already successfully verified over 1400 multithreaded programs, including some that involve complex side effects like memory allocation. The paper's findings are consistent with previous research on DPOR-based model checkers. In countries such as India, Indonesia, and Philipines, the deadly consequences of false information have raised pressure on social media platforms to adapt strategies to mitigate this issue. In response, WhatsApp introduced limitations to message forwarding in some countries, aiming to address this problem. In this research, we aim to understand the effectiveness of this solution by investigating user behavior prior to and following the implementation of these restrictions in India. Furthermore, our findings suggest that misinformation spread is driven by a small core of active users. Based on our results, we propose three possible next steps for further research focused on developing more comprehensive solutions to address online misinformation. A statistical model is developed to estimate the prevalence of alleles in populations that experience rapid, exponential growth. This prevalence spectrum, representing the distribution of alleles by frequency within a population, serves as a fundamental characteristic of populations evolving under selection for rare alleles. To calculate the prevalence spectrum, a general supercritical branching population model is employed, and it is assumed that population dynamics can be represented through a Yule-Fenchel process. This asymptotically stationary process enables the derivation of the long-term prevalence spectrum as well as an unbiased estimator based on discrete-time observations of the population. Furthermore, simulation studies are conducted to evaluate the proposed estimator and explore its non-parametric counterpart. Crucially, this theoretical framework provides a framework for investigating how observed prevalence spectra relate to underlying population dynamics and selection mechanisms. This work has the potential to contribute to our understanding of how selection for rare alleles influences population growth and diversity. This study is an extension of a previously published study (Korolev and Payton, 2022), and it addresses concerns and questions raised by the corresponding authors of that paper. In particular, this study addresses their inquiry about how to quantify rare-allele dynamics in rapidly growing populations. To effectively combat voice spoofing, we introduce an end-to-end system built on deep neural networks. This system is comprised of a victim network, induced by the speaker, and a countermeasure system. We propose the Attentive Activation Mechanism (AAM) for incorporating contextual awareness and filtering capabilities into the victim network, making it easier to distinguish genuine from forged voices. By utilizing AAM in conjunction with the countermeasure system, we achieve substantial improvements in accuracy, with a notable increase in detection rates relative to existing systems in the field, particularly on the ASVspoof 2019 dataset. Furthermore, our study highlights the dynamic nature of speaker-specific characteristics within the activation maps, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our system in identifying induced voices through contextual analysis of these maps. Finally, we showcase the system's ability to effectively mitigate voice spoofing attacks across multiple domains, including English, Mandarin, and Arabic, underscoring the system's linguistic-independent capabilities. By integrating the Standard Model of particle physics with locally supersymmetric theories, we develop a theoretical framework for inflationary phenomena, addressing two key concerns raised by the models so far explored in the literature: (a) the issue of quantum instability and (b) the need for additional matter fields that could contradict observational data on cosmological inflation. We show that in supergravity models based on the SU(2) group, a single Higgs field can effectively mitigate the high-energy problems and satisfy the inflationary and cosmological requirements concurrently. Additionally, by incorporating a soft SUSY breaking term, the scalar potential's behavior can be modified, allowing for more stringent tests of the theory against inflationary model-specific predictions. Finally, we outline possible experimental pathways to verify the underlying supersymmetry theory, provided the models we've developed are viable. Furthermore, we've made a publicly available code through Mathematica, called SSGinflation, to assist in computing the scalar potentials of supergravity models, enabling users to easily enter their own model specifications and obtain results.

A growing concern with mobile device data privacy is being addressed by Federated Learning (FL), which enables machine learning model development while maintaining data privacy, by allowing a central server to aggregate local model updates from mobile devices with their associated data. FL is particularly beneficial due to the diverse data environments and increased data security. In this research, we tackle a key FL challenge, where devices encounter unfamiliar data classes during training. To address this issue, we propose a zero-shot training approach, starting with a central server that develops a novel layer to combine existing category embeddings from mobile devices, using available classes. Then, each device optimizes its local model, incorporating a novel embedding for its local classes, while the central server optimizes the novel layer. Our approach's effectiveness is validated through audio classification experiments using two open-source datasets, resulting in comparable performance to traditional local training methods, with increased model generalability and adaptable to various data labeling schemes. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyin-lyu/zero-shot_FL. Additionally, the FL demo can be accessed via https://zero-shot-federated-training.github.io/. Furthermore, the dataset used in this research can be found at https://lyu-zhengyin.gitlab.io/zero-shot-Fed-Art dataset. Lastly, the video explaining our research can be accessed via https://lyu-zhengyin.gitlab.io/20230420-Zhengyin Lyu - Federated Learning.mp4.

This research investigates how regional news outlets in the U.S. respond to the COVID-19 pandemic in terms of coverage, case and death rates, and audience size. A multidimensional analysis framework is applied to 35 metropolitan areas across the country, utilizing data from nearly 300 local news websites and the COVID Tracking Project. Our results show that regions with higher COVID incidence receive more news coverage, with deaths having a weaker correlation. Moreover, our findings suggest that English-language news predominates in many areas, particularly in regions not adequately covered by local news. Notably, regions with lower audience sizes for local news tend to receive more news coverage, implying a trade-off between news provision and audience reach. These outcomes have significant practical implications for public health communication and news dissemination strategies, particularly when it comes to vulnerable populations who may rely more heavily on local news. Ultimately, enhancing local news reach could facilitate more effective COVID-related news coverage, ultimately saving lives. Based on these conclusions, we suggest several avenues for further research, including the exploration of additional COVID-related variables and the examination of other health topics. Additionally, we outline potential research collaborations between communication and computational scholars to develop data-driven, theory-informed studies that can harness the analytical strength of large datasets while maintaining the contextual insights inherent to local news. With these goals in mind, we make available our code and data for replication at https://github.com/LocalNewsLab/covid-local-news. A proposed ensemble of AutoRegressive, Moving Average, and Moving Minimum models can effectively forecast market patterns. To validate our approach, we compare it to traditional time-series analysis and machine learning techniques, and find that our model outperforms these methods with a significant 34% improvement in accuracy when tested on the NYSE market data. This research presents FLVoogd, a robust and Privacy-preserving Federated Learning framework. At the local level, FLVoogd employs differential privacy and generates encrypted models using homomorphic encryption. It also utilizes graph-based clustering to establish a dynamic network of trusted groups within the distributed system. We tested FLVoogd using the IMDB dataset and evaluated its performance under various scenarios. Our experiments demonstrate that FLVoogd offers enhanced resilience and Privacy preservation capabilities when compared to existing FL methods. Achieving real-world success with autonomous navigation systems poses a significant challenge due to the sim2real disconnect. This issue is exacerbated by the diverse range of driving tasks, which complicates training and model replication across platforms. To overcome this challenge, we developed a task-oriented approach that enables exposure to a broad spectrum of driving tasks, allowing for more effective training and model adaptation. This is accomplished by leveraging camera image processing to accurately replicate real-world vehicle movement, including steering and speed, within simulated environments. Additionally, our system incorporates a self-correcting mechanism to ensure seamless sim2real model transitions. The efficacy of our approach was demonstrated in various driving scenarios, where we successfully replicated real-world vehicle behavior in simulated environments. This was facilitated by developing a gradient-based training metric that captures task-specific vehicle interactions with its environment. As a result, our system can learn and adapt to a wide range of driving tasks, from basic to complex, across diverse real-world contexts. Furthermore, our approach eliminates the need for equipment costs associated with autonomous vehicle technology. This research has significant implications for advanced driver-assistance systems and the development of fully autonomous vehicles, where rapid model adaptation and exposure to various driving conditions are crucial. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/alexandreschultheiss/grads.

This research introduces a method of validating generalized polynomial chaos expansions that can capture stochastic phenomena. The proposed method leverages the properties of non-negative definite kernels to measure the accuracy of such expansions when approximating certain functions in randomized analyses. The method further provides a precise bound on the error made during the approximation process, thus enabling the refinement of expansions to achieve greater precision. The researchers applied and tested this verification method in two main scenarios: by manually adjusting the order of expansions to improve precision in non-smooth, non-periodic cases and by adapting the method to approximate functions with discontinuities. Additionally, the researchers applied the verification method to simulate non-linear stochastic problems in physics, specifically the heat conduction equation with varying coefficients and the 3D ground-water flow equation, to illustrate its effectiveness in high-dimensional contexts. The refinement process resulted in significant reductions in computational costs associated with these simulations. The research demonstrates that the proposed verification method can efficiently improve the precision of generalized polynomial chaos expansions while minimizing computational costs. The vast array of dwarf galaxies provides an ideal opportunity to expand our understanding of the initial conditions of the universe, allowing us to refine cosmological models and shed light on the processes that shaped galaxy evolution.  By analyzing chemical compositions and the life cycles of stars within these dwarf galaxies, scientists can gain valuable insights into the universe's early development.  Through a comprehensive analysis of 15 low-mass galaxies, researchers investigated the creation of light elements, the formation of stars, and the characteristics of their Galactic Winds.  Their findings suggest that these low-mass galaxies produce between 1% and 10% of the necessary heavy elements required for life to emerge, primarily through supernovae explosions that inject elements into space.  By estimating the mass of gas that escapes into space, scientists can evaluate the effectiveness of Galactic Winds in regulating chemical compositions and shaping galaxy evolution.  Further investigation into dwarf galaxies is necessary to refine theoretical models and ensure that they accurately replicate the diversity of galaxies we observe today.  By combining numerical simulations with observational data, scientists can develop a more comprehensive understanding of the universe's early development and the processes that formed our cosmic neighborhood.  Ultimately, this research will help answer the fundamental question of how the universe's initial conditions gave rise to the diverse array of galaxies we see around us today.

Inspired by the concept of homotopy invariants developed by Jonathan Smith, we introduce a homotopy action spectrum for profinite groups, derived from their finite group homologies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our homotopy action spectrum serves as a universal system in which to express $\mathbb{Q}$-valued homotopy invariants for finite groups, and also investigate its applicability to cyclic and $2$-groups in particular. Lastly, in the case of a profinite group acting faithfully on a topological space, we establish a connection between its homotopy action spectrum and the homotopy theory of the group, as formulated by Jonathan Smith, revealing a rich set of relationships between these two theories. Ultimately, our study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the homotopy theory of profinite groups, encompassing both $\mathbb{Q}$-valued and integer-valued aspects. In addition, we believe that the homotopy action spectrum of a profinite group will serve as a versatile tool with diverse applications across multiple fields, including algebraic topology, algebraic geometry, and number theory. A recent surge in the creation of visually appealing documents has underscored the importance of an efficient text extraction technique for a wide range of applications, including both commercial and research contexts. Although machine learning has significantly enhanced the accuracy of text extraction from documents, the manual process of data labeling for training models becomes prohibitively expensive as the amount of data increases. To address this challenge, our proposed framework, called LEA, leverages domain knowledge on a small, initial dataset to automatically generate more labeled data, thereby reducing the reliance on manual labeling. By integrating this approach with a pre-trained model, we have developed a comprehensive text extraction solution that outperforms existing benchmarks on recent datasets by achieving comparable accuracy with significantly less manual labeling required. Furthermore, our website dedicated to document understanding now includes additional details, along with a comprehensive guide to getting started with LEA. Deep learning model pruning has become a crucial technique for deploying trimmed neural networks on devices with limited resources. However, previous studies have encountered issues during the training of pruned models, as they often experience decreased accuracy and network disruptions. There's a noticeable gap between the pruning algorithms used for inference and those for training. Most algorithms focus on removing redundant connections (parameters) during inference but don't consider the effects on computation (operations). As a result, training these models can be challenging because the focus is solely on eliminating computations, leading to disrupted models that fail to learn effectively. To bridge this gap, we introduce ClickTrain, an innovative end-to-end training framework that enables the learning of pruned neural networks while preserving their original structure. By targeting parameters rather than computations, we leverage a custom loss function to guide a pattern-based pruning algorithm, ensuring a smoother and more efficient pruning process. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach and highlight its potential to create more precise and practical models for deployment. We investigated the supersymmetric quantum dynamics of a specific fermionic system using the Lagrangian approach, resulting in first-order differential equations that describe its time evolution. As a result, the supersymmetric partition function can be calculated through either the direct computation of cohomology groups or the permutation expansion of a supermatrix within a specific matrix product, thus illustrating the equivalence between supersymmetric quantum mechanics and the matrix model representation of the sheaf cohomology expansion. Additionally, we derived a general formula for the supersymmetric partition function of the oscillator system, validated by numerical integration of the differential equations, and observed that certain superfields exhibit duality symmetry in specific cases. Finally, we proposed future research directions, including generalizing our approach to systems with extended supersymmetry and exploring the connection to quantum field theory through the double-point limit. Furthermore, we suggest investigating perfect complexes within quantum mechanics and supersymmetric quantum mechanics, as well as applying our method to the study of Wilson loops via supersymmetric quantum mechanics and sheaf cohomology. This study presents the approaches employed by the UM-IU@LING system team at SemEval 2019 in addressing two sub-tasks of OffensEval (Classifying and Identifying Subcategories of Offensive Text). The competition aimed to recognize toxic and derogatory content within social media posts. Our strategy for sub-task A entailed training and combining three different classifiers using various social media data sets, along with two additional models leveraging BERT. For sub-task B, we applied a one-vs-all SVM approach utilizing 119 categories from the provided data set. Furthermore, we assessed the effectiveness of combining the two models on the test data set. Ultimately, our submissions yielded the second-best and third-best results among all competitors for sub-task A and sub-task B, respectively. Computed tomography (CT) is a widely used technique in various medical and industrial applications for imaging dense objects and identifying multiple materials based on distinct energy characteristics. However, actual CT scanners produce images under the assumption of a single energy source, which leads to double refraction and image degradation. Furthermore, measurement errors during data collection also compromise image quality. To overcome these challenges, we present a novel non-convex approach that simultaneously handles polyenergetic projections, noise reduction, and material decomposition. To achieve robust solutions, we incorporate prior constraints on the material densities and a stabilized backward-forward splitting method. To evaluate our approach, we use a digital phantom that contains details on polyenergetic projections and material compositions, and we compare our results with traditional single-energy and low-dose reconstruction techniques. Our method demonstrates the ability to produce high-quality images from low-quality data and accurately decompose materials with varying densities. To validate our results, we also provide quantitative assessments using relative error metrics and a breakdown assessment using a quantitative validation phantom. Our non-convex framework can be applied to various CT applications and may be extended to other imaging modalities. The source code for our approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/romainagostini/Breakdown\_and\_denoising\_in\_polyenergetic\_CT. High-performance computing on GPUs heavily relies on efficient memory management systems to maximize memory access coherency, but current memory allocators on GPUs often neglect this aspect, leading to performance degradation. To address this limitation, we present a high-throughput memory allocator called DynaSOAr that aims to increase memory access coherency on GPUs through optimized scheduling. DynaSOAr internally divides memory into page-sized blocks, dynamically assigning them to objects of varying sizes. Its core-matching algorithm matches memory pages to objects, minimizing memory access fragmentation and improving coherency. To further enhance performance, DynaAr uses two optimization techniques: (1) tail-end merging, which reduces memory usage by combining trailing memory blocks, and (2) dynamic memory reallocation, which quickly reassigns memory pages during memory deallocation. As a result, DynaSOAr outperforms leading GPU memory allocators by at least 1.3 times and shows potential for other parallel programming environments. To address the origin of dark matter, we modify the $U(1)_X$ extension of the Standard Model by introducing additional gauge symmetries, incorporating a fundamental $X$ field, a VEV of a scalar doublet, and a Di-photon operator. Within the framework of Standard Model left-right symmetry, we establish lower bounds on the $B$-$L$ scale using Higgs mass and dark matter relic density constraints. A notable influence of the $SU(2)_L$ and $SU(2)_R$ symmetries on the gauge boson masses is observed, leading to a correction in the $U(1)_X$ mass scale. Furthermore, incorporating a fundamental $X$ field into the Georgi-Manton mechanism yields minimal, non-trivial vortex solutions with varying $X$ field profiles, thereby inducing an irreducible dark matter spin-1 component. A possible dark matter mass range arises from a $SU(2) \times U(1)$ invariant confining theory, where an $X$ boson mediates the interaction. Additionally, a dark photon exchange between the scalar doublet and fermion fields generates a dark matter mass and gives rise to dark charged sectors. Lastly, an anomaly-free $U(1)_X$ combination is presented that accommodates a dark matter candidate with mass spin-1 properties. Several experimental tests for the $U(1)_X$ and its associated sector are proposed. Finally, an outline of potential future research is given to further investigate the characteristics of Standard Model and its dark matter extension. Specifically, an examination of the scalar sector, dark matter coupling, and gauge boson mass sum rules is suggested. The tube's internal void space is 1.5 cm in diameter. The measurements revealed that this value applies broadly to tubes with 1 mm and thicker within the specified range of 20-1000 K. When generating uncertainty reports for complex systems, the conventional method involves establishing a reliability guarantee through Bayesian network analysis, similar to sturdiness assurance, for a specified confidence level. The traditional approach faces obstacles due to its limited applicability and the difficulty in modeling, although it provides strong assurances. In contrast, the Markov chain Monte Carlo method is more adaptable and efficient in modeling, but only offers a posterior distribution without any reliability guarantee. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a new method that ensures a minimum level of sturdiness for probabilistic circuits while maintaining a low error rate in the computation of posterior probabilities. This method can be applied to various probabilistic models, including Bayesian networks and belief distributions, and provides a lower bound on sturdiness that aligns with the specified error rate. The method can be further optimized by introducing a new metric called sturdiness efficiency, which offers a trade-off between sturdiness guarantee and computational efficiency. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through case studies involving fault and performance analysis in electronic design automation. Additionally, open-source implementations are available for research reproduction through the Bayesello toolset. Open issues and potential future research directions are also discussed. Furthermore, a supplementary document provides more detailed information on the sturdiness efficiency metric, its variations, and the open-source implementation. The rotation measure of the galactic center's molecular gas arrangement, specifically in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), has long been debated. By analyzing data from the ATCA and VLA, we generated two-dimensional maps for nine distinct molecular species, which showed a consistent pattern rotated approximately 50 degrees compared to the larger ring structure formed by these molecules. We developed an approach to measure the rotation and spatial variations within these maps, which revealed that some species exhibit little to no rotation while others show up to 100 km/s per parsec. The species showing the most extreme rotation, namely CH$_3$OH and H$_2$CO, are primarily composed of neutral gas, suggesting that their emission is not heavily influenced by ionized gas emission as initially thought. The rotation of the CMZ, along with its radial and vertical structures, can be explained by the gas arrangement in the larger ring structure being turned inside out, with the species' rotation rates closely correlated with this arrangement. This discovery provides further evidence for the CMZ's rotation, which has been observed in various forms, and offers a new perspective on the galactic center's complex and dynamic environment. The interaction between delocalized electrons and localized holes in amorphous solids is the root cause of delayed absorption phenomena observed in x-ray absorption near edge spectra, particularly evident in non-linear high-intensity x-ray ABS. We have devised a rate equation model based on the concept of electron groups to describe the initial events following core excitation, taking into account the effects of electron-electron scattering and electron-hole interaction. The onset of electronic excitation occurs when the ground state energy equilibrium is disrupted, giving rise to electron groups characterized by increasing energy levels. The rate at which electrons transition from lower to higher energy states is influenced by the electron-hole interaction and electron-electron scattering, as well as the density of states available. We have calculated absorption rates as a function of photon energy and delay time, utilizing the average group velocity of electron groups to bridge linear and non-linear x-ray ABS phenomena. The model's accuracy has been validated through comparisons with experimental data on Ar, Ne, and N$_2$ and the results demonstrate its capability to provide in-depth insights into the underlying electronic excitation processes. Furthermore, the model's versatility can be adapted to describe non-linear high-intensity x-ray ABS in other solids. We believe that the proposed model will significantly contribute to the understanding of initial electronic excitation events and subsequent relaxation processes. Additionally, the model's rate-based approach has the potential to facilitate high-throughput computational simulations, thereby facilitating the development of novel materials with optimized x-ray ABS properties. We envision that the model will stimulate collaborative research at the intersection of materials science, high-intensity x-ray physics, and computational algorithm design. The model's computational framework is freely accessible online at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/rahulsharma-iitb/xrayabs.git. The code can be run to generate absorption spectra in line with the model's predictions, as shown in the present study and earlier research on linear high-intensity x-ray ABS. We are confident that the proposed model will stimulate innovative research in x-ray ABS and accelerate the development of novel materials exhibiting optimized high-intensity x-ray ABS characteristics. This research introduces a low-voltage and high-accuracy temperature sensor built using a standard CMOS process, which can operate within a wide voltage range of 0.6 to 1.8 volts. The proposed temperature detector incorporates a bipolar junction transistor that serves as a temperature-dependent transistor, utilizing the native temperature-dependent threshold voltage of the transistor to provide a temperature coefficient of 104.1mV/degC. The system's temperature sensitivity is enhanced by incorporating a digital temperature compensation technique based on a binary search method. As a result, the overall temperature resolution reaches an impressive 0.24degC precision, with only a 1.06nJ energy consumption per conversion. Moreover, the system's error associated with temperature tracking is limited to no more than 1.4degC error. To facilitate the use of this design in wearable technology and similar applications, its area is kept relatively small, with a footprint of 0.0625mm^2. The system's functionality was thoroughly verified using simulations, which confirmed its compatibility with weak and weakless systems. The temperature sensor's voltage-independent output also simplifies its integration into diverse systems. We have devised Internet-compatible spanners with constant stretch and logarithmic diameter, for networks simulating random geometric distributions of nodes with varying connectivity. Furthermore, our work addresses the existing challenges in Internet-based geometric spanners by incorporating two key aspects – simplicity and efficiency. The complexity of our constructions is significantly reduced, yielding efficient protocols applicable in real-time scenarios. The efficiency of our protocols is optimized by limiting the number of packet transmissions required. We achieve this by leveraging Delaunay triangulation and developing a novel approach for identifying shallow nodes in a highly efficient manner, thereby reducing the number of packet transmissions to nearly O(log^2 n) per node. The detailed analysis and simulations of our methods indicate that they can produce spanners with constant stretch for large node populations with as little as 7 packet transmissions per node on average. We have successfully tested and validated our protocols in an experimental setup featuring nodes arranged in a uniform pattern over two-dimensional space. The results show that our protocols can produce and utilize spanners with constant stretch in real-time, even when subjected to packet transmission variability. The source code for our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/compnetsec/Internet-Euclidean-Spanner.
